title: Agent Marketplace
content: Agent Marketplace The agent marketplace is a catalog of community-built agents hosted on GitHub. Agav reads the catalog when you open the Marketplace tab and lets you install agents directly into your global or project configuration. Opening the marketplace The marketplace tab fetches from the configured marketplace URL and displays all available agents. Browsing agents Agents are displayed three per page. Navigate with: | Key / mouse | Action | | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | | / , mouse wheel, hover, left-click | Move selection within the current page | | / | Previous / next page | | | Open search — filter by name, description, category, or tag | | | Inspect selected agent (shows tools, credentials, and description) | | | Refresh from the marketplace URL | | | Update the selected agent to the latest marketplace version | | | Install the selected agent | | | Clear search / exit | Agents already installed on your system show a or badge. Installing an agent Select an agent and press . If the agent is not yet installed, a destination prompt appears: Press or to install. If the agent is already installed at project scope, pressing offers to promote it to global (removes the project copy and reinstalls globally). Globally installed agents block re-installation at project scope — use the List tab to manage them instead. Configuring after install After installing, switch to the List tab to configure credentials: The config editor shows each required credential with its current status ( or ). Press on a field to edit it, paste your value, and press again to save. Values are encrypted at rest. CLI installation Install without opening the TUI: CLI HTTP(S) installs clone a Git repository and require on ; a marketplace’s raw file URL is not a Git clone URL. Use the Marketplace tab to install from an HTTP file catalog. CLI Git URLs are restricted to these hosts: github.com, gitlab.com, bitbucket.org, and raw.githubusercontent.com. Set (comma-separated) to allow additional hosts. Agent names must start with a letter or digit and contain only letters, digits, dots, hyphens, or underscores (max 64 characters). > Windows: paths resolve to . Local marketplace For local development and testing, clone the marketplace repo and set: On Windows, use a drive-letter URL such as . Use a directory path without spaces for the local TUI catalog: it does not decode percent-encoded paths. takes precedence over ; the environment variable replaces the built-in default when no config value is set. Hosting a marketplace Use a static file server or a raw GitHub content URL as the catalog base. A GitHub repository’s normal browser URL serves HTML, not . For HTTP installs, each catalog entry must include , an explicit list relative to the entry’s (for example, ). The minimum structure: See the official marketplace repository for a complete example. Deleting agents When a globally installed, user-created agent (one without a marketplace ) is deleted from the List or Create tab, Agav automatically saves it as a template before removal. Project-scoped user-created agents are deleted without a template. The template preserves the agent's name, description, system prompt, MCP server selections, and tags. You can restore it later from the Create tab (). Marketplace agents (those installed from a URL) are deleted without creating a template — they can be reinstalled from the marketplace at any time. title: Agents
content: Agents Agents are named, purpose-built sub-agents that extend Agav with domain-specific capabilities. Each agent has its own tool set, system prompt, and isolated credentials. When your query involves a task an agent handles — listing GitHub PRs, searching Jira tickets, taking a screenshot — the LLM routes to it automatically. How agents work When Agav starts, it loads all enabled agents and registers each one as a callable tool. The LLM reads a compact catalog (one line per agent, capped at ~500 tokens total) and chooses the right agent for the task. An agent invocation runs a nested agent loop with the agent's tools, system prompt, and credentials, with a separate conversation and tool registry. Results stream back to you normally. Loading order Agav discovers agents from three locations. Later tiers override earlier ones by name, so you can replace a bundled agent with a custom version: | Tier | Location | Override priority | | --- | --- | --- | | Bundled | Shipped with Agav binary (currently empty — reserved for future built-in agents) | Lowest | | Global | | Middle | | Project | in the working directory | Highest | > Windows: paths resolve to . Installing agents from the marketplace Browse and install agents from the community marketplace: See Agent Marketplace for full details. Creating agents You can create custom agents directly from the TUI without writing a manifest by hand: The Create tab opens a "My Agents" hub that lists your user-created agents and any saved templates. From here you can create a new agent or restore one from a template. Wizard flow Selecting New Agent launches a five-step wizard: 1. Name & Description — pick a unique agent name and a short description of what it does. 2. System Prompt — write the agent's system prompt, or press to auto-generate one. The LLM uses your name and description to draft a prompt you can edit before continuing. 3. Native Tools — select the built-in Agav tools the agent can use. This creates the manifest's allowlist; leave every option unchecked if the agent should use only its local and MCP tools. 4. MCP Servers — select which MCP servers the agent should have access to. The list is populated from your workspace config ( in or ). 5. Review & Save — preview the full agent definition and confirm. The agent is saved to and immediately available for use. Templates When you delete a user-created agent, Agav automatically saves it as a template so you can recreate it later without starting from scratch. - Templates appear in the Create tab's "My Agents" list with a label. - Opening a template pre-populates the wizard with the original name, description, system prompt, and MCP server selections — edit anything before saving. - Press on a template in the list to remove it permanently. - Templates are stored in . Per-agent MCP servers Native agents can declare stdio MCP servers in their manifest. The wizard can copy command-based servers from workspace configuration. It does not import URL-only HTTP/SSE entries, and subsequent edits preserve the agent’s saved server settings rather than resyncing them. See per-agent MCP fields for environment precedence and tool selection. Servers are started when the agent runs and stopped when it finishes — their tools are scoped to that invocation. The server process itself is not sandboxed by the agent-tool runner. Credentials Each agent declares the environment variables it needs ( in the manifest). Credentials are: - Saved encrypted by the config editor in inside the installed agent directory. Don’t commit a project agent’s . - Passed to native tools at runtime and to any stdio MCP servers declared by that agent. MCP subprocesses also inherit Agav’s launch environment. - Editable from the agent inspect view: Agents with missing credentials show a indicator in the List tab. The LLM receives an error message if it tries to call an unconfigured agent. Tool permissions and confirmation The manifest can classify tools as or . In mode, marking an agent-local or MCP tool does not exempt it from confirmation. Trusted built-ins retain their normal permission rules. refuses tool calls that still require confirmation. See Security. Native tool access Native agents do not automatically receive Agav's built-in tools. Select the tools they need during creation, or open and edit Native Tools. The chosen tools are written to the agent's manifest allowlist. Leaving the list empty keeps built-in tools unavailable while preserving agent-local and declared MCP tools. Bundled and A2A agents cannot edit this setting. Agent sandbox Non-bundled agent-local JavaScript runs in a subprocess. On macOS with Seatbelt or Linux with Bubblewrap, it uses a separate profile that blocks networking. On Windows, or when neither supported agent backend is available, it runs without OS sandboxing. The Windows restricted-token and Docker shell backends do not cover these tools, and does not make them fail closed. Built-ins such as keep their own policy; per-agent MCP and A2A processes do not use the agent-tool profile. Install only code you trust. Model and effort overrides Agents inherit the session's model and effort by default. You can override them per-agent in the config editor (). The override is stored in the agent's and shown as in the inspect view. Clear the value to revert to inheriting from the session. CLI TUI Open to manage agents interactively. The three tabs are: - * — view, inspect, enable/disable, and remove installed agents. - — browse and install community agents. - * — create new agents with the wizard, and manage your agents and templates. The tabs and visible list rows can be selected with a left-click. In list and marketplace views, the mouse wheel moves the selection; resource-manager footer controls such as search, inspect, and refresh are clickable when enabled. Keyboard shortcuts remain available as a fallback, and clicks do not bypass confirmation prompts. Related - Agent Marketplace — browse and install community agents - Agent Manifest reference — full AGENT.md format - Build a Native Agent — write your own agent - Install and Configure an Agent — step-by-step walkthrough - Build an Agent from a Template — restore and customize a saved template

title: Background jobs
content: Background jobs Background jobs are an opt-in subsystem for commands that must keep running after the agent's turn ends, such as dev servers, long builds, and watchers. They can also be launched on a cron schedule. The agent starts and manages them with the tool; you inspect and control them with . To leave an agent conversation running rather than a shell command, see Detached sessions. The same flag enables worker-owned ordinary interactive prompts when set before submitting the task; no separate opt-in is needed. and manage the conversation; manages shell jobs. Enable it in : While the flag is unset or , and refuse every action. > Background jobs are not sandboxed. Jobs launched through run with : full access as your OS user, outside the Seatbelt, Bubblewrap, Windows restricted-token, and Docker sandboxes available to , and without its 30-second timeout. Read the confirmation prompt before approving. What a job is Each job is a shell command run by a small detached supervisor process, so it keeps running when Agav exits. Agav stores job state, grants, and captured output under ( on Windows). - States: a job moves through , , and , then ends as , , or . If Agav cannot establish the truth after a crash it reports or with a reason; it never reports success without evidence. - Output: stdout and stderr are captured separately and can be read while the job is still running. - Limits: at most 4 jobs run at once. Further starts are refused rather than queued. - Supervisor lifetime: a finished job's supervisor stays up for about five minutes to serve and , then exits on its own. - Descendants: on macOS and Linux, a job can stay after its shell exits while descendants in the owned process group are still running. Windows shell jobs do not provide that guarantee. - Stopping: where group ownership is available, signals the owned group and escalates if needed. Processes that escape the group are not tracked. On Windows, the reported stop covers only the top-level process; descendant status can remain unverified. Choose ( or ) and for only the last N bytes; the default is the first 64 KiB. | | | Block until a job is terminal. Cancelling the turn ends the wait, not the job. | | | Request termination of one job. | | , , | Manage recurring schedules (see below). | Use for and ; optional defaults to Agav’s working directory. also requires and . Use for , , , or ; unambiguous prefixes are accepted. Use an exact for . command | Command | Purpose | | --- | --- | | | Open the interactive manager. Tab switches between Jobs and Schedules. | | | Show all known jobs. | | | Show the state of one job. | | | Show stdout (default) or stderr; returns the last N bytes. | | | Request termination of one job. | | | Show schedules. | | | Register a recurring command. | | | Permanently stop a schedule from launching. | | | Release capacity for an eligible unverified job without stopping it or deleting its evidence. | | | Show what this platform can enforce. | cannot start a one-off job; ask the agent to use . In the manager, the job list shows each job’s command and directory, and search matches both. Press to stop an eligible job. In the Schedules tab, creates a schedule, pauses or resumes it, revokes it, and deletes an eligible inactive schedule and its run history without deleting the jobs it launched. Use abandonment only after inspecting an unverified job and its side effects. It releases accounting capacity and prevents a future startup of that job, but does not stop any process, verify the outcome, or authorize a retry. The manager offers for eligible jobs and to show or hide retained abandoned evidence. The shell equivalent of the slash command is . Press uppercase in either list and confirm with to permanently delete finished jobs (including their logs) and eligible paused or revoked schedules (including their run history) across both tabs. This ignores search filters. Active or uncertain jobs, abandoned job evidence, enabled schedules, and schedules with an active job or pending launch are kept. , , and show the approval prompt inline in the interactive app. During an active turn, , , , , , and can run without switching views. A targeted stop still requires its normal authorization. If approval cannot be shown inline, a busy session returns instructions rather than opening the manager. An idle session can open the manager for you to take the action there; the original action is not re-run. An unknown or ambiguous job ID is reported as an error and never opens the manager. shows the first 64 KiB of retained stdout by default. Use with a positive whole number of bytes for the end of the stream. For a job that failed, it also appends the exit code and its stderr, so you do not have to rerun with . Passing or shows only that stream. On normal interactive exit, Agav reports jobs it verifies are active separately from jobs with unverified status. An unverified job may still be running. Finished and abandoned jobs are omitted. Approval and permission modes Starting a job, creating a schedule, stopping a job, and revoking a schedule are each a separate approved action. The prompt shows the full command, the working directory, the isolation level (flagged when unrestricted), and for schedules the cron expression and timezone. Approvals are reusable. Approving a spec covers that exact command, directory, and isolation (and for schedules, the cron and timezone) for that action. Changing any of them asks again. An approved schedule can launch future runs without prompting each time, subject to its state and the current automation policy. | Mode | Behavior | | --- | --- | | | Prompts for each action that has no existing approval. | | | Approves automatically. Use only in trusted workflows. | | | Refuses new jobs and new schedules. Stopping a job and revoking or pausing a schedule still prompt, so you can always shut down existing work. Resuming a paused schedule is refused. | In print and mode no one can answer a prompt, so these actions are refused unless an explicit grant already covers them. A model cannot opt out of this through tool arguments. Recurring schedules A schedule launches its command on a five-field cron expression in an IANA timezone, for example . Wildcard steps start at the field's minimum, so day-of-month matches the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and so on. Enter these examples inside Agav, not at your shell prompt. On macOS and Linux, jobs run via : On Windows, invoke Windows PowerShell explicitly for PowerShell commands: On Windows the job runner defaults to even if you start Agav from PowerShell. It does not translate shell syntax. Otherwise, use syntax. - Fixed at approval. The working directory is resolved to an absolute path and the environment is captured when you create the schedule, then both are covered by the approval. A run uses exactly that directory and environment, regardless of which session or process triggers it. - One active job per schedule. If the previous run is still going, the next occurrence is skipped. - No catch-up. A missed occurrence is not queued or backfilled. - Revoking is permanent. It blocks future launches only; jobs already launched keep running. A revoked schedule stays listed as revoked. Pausing is reversible. - sessions pause launches. While a connected session is in , schedules do not fire. When schedules are evaluated By default, schedules are checked about every 30 seconds only while an interactive Agav session with is running. Closing Agav stops evaluation. To fire schedules while Agav is closed, configure unattended automation explicitly. It reads only the global config and never creates project files. | Command | Behavior | | --- | --- | | | Evaluate due schedules once and exit. | | | Register an OS entry that evaluates schedules every minute: systemd timer or cron on Linux, a LaunchAgent on macOS, a scheduled task on Windows. | | | Show the entry. Exits if installed, if not. Reinstall if reported stale or outdated. | | | Remove the entry. Job state on disk is kept. | | | Run a foreground daemon that ticks every 15 seconds until interrupted. | | | Stop the running daemon. | | | Exits if running, if not. | Set in the global config to suspend background schedule evaluation without uninstalling the OS entry or stopping the daemon. This also pauses the interactive background schedule ticker; it does not cancel running jobs and is ignored in project config. Unattended runs have no one to prompt, so they launch only schedules you already approved. An interactive session and an unattended host can run together; the same occurrence is never launched twice. Completion notifications Completion events are recorded when a job finishes, but Agav does not yet show them. No automatic "job finished" notification is delivered. Check on a job with , , , or the manager. Platform notes Run to see what your platform reports. Linux and macOS own a process group per job. Windows has no Job Object tree ownership in this release, so stopping a job may leave child processes running. Unattended automation needs a filesystem that supports hard links; without it, Agav refuses to reserve a schedule occurrence rather than risk launching it twice. See also Automation for session loops, , and , and Security for the trust model.

An omitted bound uses the first or last cell, respectively. An end past the last cell is clamped; a start past the last cell is an error. Range results report the cells actually read and the notebook's total cell count. A range on an empty notebook reports that there are no cells. Set to , , or to filter cells within the selected range. The default, , includes every cell type. Filtered results keep their original cell numbers. Cached text output is included by default; set to return just the selected cells’ source and metadata such as cell numbers and types. is off by default. Enable it per session with the [](/reference/cli) flag, or turn it on by default with the field in configuration. Search requests time out after 30 seconds and report an error rather than waiting indefinitely. The optional argument accepts integers from 1 to 30 and defaults to 8. The tool may return fewer results if the provider returns fewer matches. Connected MCP servers, installed plugins, and active skills can add more tools. Output limits and recovery Tool text returned through Agav's registry is limited to 40,000 UTF-8 bytes and 2,000 lines, including truncation notices. This also covers registered MCP, plugin, skill, and subagent results, errors, and text appended by hooks. Small results are unchanged. Oversized results normally keep a head/tail excerpt with an explicit omission notice; image blocks, error status, and structured result metadata are preserved. Text limits do not cap image token usage. These are fixed implementation limits, not provider-token counts. There is no parameter on , , or , and no configuration setting to raise these limits. Narrow the query or retrieve a specific saved section instead. Saved output paths and retention When output is saved, the notice gives the actual absolute path. The layout is: Agav writes first and publishes by atomic rename. On Unix, directories use mode and files use . Logs can contain private command output or API response data; private permissions are not encryption. - Each saved file holds at most 16 MiB. A partial-log notice means only a prefix was saved, not all omitted content. - Each Agav process has a 128 MiB retention budget, including reservations for unfinished writes, and at most 4,096 capture admissions. Shell and HTTP captures reserve 16 MiB each while pending; publication releases unused reserved bytes. - The per-user temporary root admits 32 process slots, reserving up to 4 GiB of payload capacity across processes sharing that root (plus metadata). - Published logs are not evicted during a live process. Orderly process exit attempts to delete that process's slot, so these paths are not durable session-history attachments. Copy any log you need before exiting Agav. - After a crash, a later startup or first capture can prune a slot only when its recorded creation time is at least 24 hours old and its owner PID is confirmed dead. This is an opportunistic sweep, not a timer or guaranteed 24-hour deletion. Live or reused PIDs, denied probes, unsafe paths, and unknown ownership metadata are conservatively left alone. If storage is full, unavailable, unsafe, or over quota, Agav returns a bounded warning rather than advertising a nonexistent log. Saving failure does not change the original tool's success/error status or rerun its side effects; omitted content may be unavailable. Use the path in the notice with and /, or with a targeted pattern. Recovery calls are bounded too. If uses its JavaScript fallback (always used on Windows), it skips files larger than 1 MiB; use line-range reads or a targeted shell search for larger logs. A saved “complete returned text” file contains what the tool returned, not data the tool already excluded or summarized. In particular, the test runner's raw diagnostic excerpt is not a complete test-process transcript. File reads and repository maps can be absolute or relative to the working directory. Text ranges use 1-based, inclusive and . If only is provided, reading starts at line 1; if only is provided, reading continues toward EOF until the output limit. Ends beyond EOF are clamped, while a start beyond EOF is an error. Invalid or reversed ranges are rejected. For text, set explicitly to , , , or ; omit it for the default UTF-8 detection. Include the same encoding when continuing a ranged read. Large text files are streamed rather than loaded in full. A bounded text read returns a contiguous prefix of the requested range, reserving room for headers and recovery instructions (at most 1,995 selected whole lines). Its continuation notice identifies the next in the original file, preserving any requested ; no duplicate temporary copy is needed. Follow that notice rather than treating the returned excerpt as the whole file. If the first requested line alone is too long, Agav returns a bounded excerpt and recommends targeted byte extraction with ; repeating that same line range will not advance through the line. PDF and Office ranges use 1-based, inclusive and , with at most 10 pages per preview. Images do not accept line or page ranges, and PDF/Office documents do not accept line ranges. Office fallback behavior depends on available conversion tools: without LibreOffice, uses extracted slide text, while uses extracted text without preserving page ranges or visual layout. See files and context for attachment and preview requirements; attachment limits are separate from these tool-result limits. Use and (integers from 0 to 50) to show surrounding lines. Matches keep the format, context lines use , overlapping windows are merged, and separates non-adjacent groups. still counts matches only. Context cannot be combined with unless both context counts are zero. Both and skip common generated and dependency directories during traversal: , , , , , , , and . To search one of these locations, specify it (or a path inside it) explicitly as . Structured test runs and verification supports , , , , and . It detects the framework from the working directory, or accepts a override. selects a test target, not a new working directory; Cargo treats it as a test-name filter. If detection fails, specify the framework or use for the project's own test script. uses the same auto-detected OS sandbox, network policy, credential filtering, and enforcement as . It has no parameter or Docker override. If a required sandbox is unavailable or cannot launch, tests are refused without an unsandboxed retry. The test process defaults to a 120-second timeout; set to an integer from 1 to 600,000 (10 minutes) to override it. A timeout is a failure even if partial output shows passing tests. The runner has a 1 MiB output-buffer limit per stream, separate from 's streaming capture. Results show framework and actual test pass/fail counts, up to ten highlighted failures, and short traceback excerpts. Failed or inconclusive runs also show the last 2,000 characters of raw output, plus any process error; this is not a full log. Agav attaches structured verification metadata with , , , , and : | Status | Meaning | | --- | --- | | | Normal zero exit, positive recognized passing-test count, and no recognized failures/errors | | | Nonzero exit, spawn/startup error, timeout/signal, or recognized test failures/errors — even if some tests passed | | | Zero exit but no recognized passing tests (for example, zero tests, skipped-only tests, or unrecognized output) | is null when the process did not exit normally. JavaScript counts come from test summaries rather than suite/file counts; pytest counts come from its result summary rather than warning text; Cargo counts include all recognized suite summaries. An inconclusive result can be non-error, but it is not evidence of successful verification. Merely returning text such as “Passed: 10” without structured metadata is not enough either. A passing in a later tool batch than a successful or counts toward Agav's post-edit verification guard, avoiding redundant “you did not verify” requests. New successful edits invalidate earlier evidence. An edit and check in the same parallel batch do not establish post-edit verification, regardless of result order. Failure wins when multiple checks share a batch; a later passing batch can reverify. Existing shell-check recognition, permissions, hooks, and capped test-repair prompts remain in place; failed edit calls alone do not count as successful modifications, and hook output does not verify an edit. Passing tests do not replace a task-required build, manual run, broader regression checks, warning review, or comparison against expected output. When output is truncated, retrieve the relevant saved sections or use a focused diagnostic command before concluding that warnings and errors are resolved. Context and cost Bounded outputs and focused reads reduce oversized text sent back to the model, but recovery calls add context and may require further model requests. Agav's base instructions also consolidate repeated verification guidance without relaxing the requirements to test after edits, check regressions, build/run/check output, and investigate every warning. These changes do not alter model or effort defaults, remove tools, or change compaction behavior. Byte reductions and avoided redundant verification rounds are not guaranteed billing or throughput savings: tokenization, prompt caching, task scope, and follow-up retrieval all affect the result. Language-server navigation The tool can find definitions, references, and hover information in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, and Go projects when the matching language-server executable is available. | Language | Executable | | --- | --- | | TypeScript or JavaScript | | | Python | | | Rust | | | Go | | Ask Agav for semantic evidence explicitly when a text search is not enough: Agav combines language-server results with file reads and repository search. If the server is unavailable, confirm that its executable is on in the shell that started Agav. Diagnostic notifications are not yet fully surfaced, so use the project's normal diagnostic command when complete output matters. GitHub operations requires the CLI to be installed and authenticated. Set to or , or omit it to use repository discovery. Use or with a positive issue or PR and non-empty . Confirmations and undo Writes, edits, and sensitive commands can display a confirmation prompt. Edit confirmations include a diff. treats replacement text literally, including dollar patterns such as . Choosing the session-wide approval option releases ordinary queued confirmations as well, but does not approve mutations that require explicit per-call consent. Agav records prior content for tracked file edits in an in-memory undo stack: The stack contains up to twenty changes and does not survive process exit. A newly created file has no previous content to restore. reverts only the change numbered in (1 is the most recent entry) and leaves newer changes in place. File boundaries The file tools (, , ) enforce path boundary checks. Writes are restricted to the working directory, temp directory, and . Reads are denied for credential stores (, , , ). Writes to and inside the project are always denied. On Windows, these paths resolve under . See security for details. Shell execution Shell commands have a 30-second default timeout ( accepts integers from 1 to 120,000) and bounded output. Agav auto-detects macOS Seatbelt, Linux Bubblewrap, or the Windows restricted-token helper (enabled by default on Windows); Docker can be requested as a override when available. The tool schema advertises the overrides available to the current session. streams stdout/stderr, so a large output no longer fails merely by exceeding the old shell buffer. Small results show stdout followed by stderr; oversized results and saved logs use observed arrival order across the two streams. Above 40,000 decoded UTF-8 bytes (or when status/separator formatting crosses that limit), it saves a log and returns a Unicode-safe head/tail preview. The shared registry can additionally truncate results exceeding 2,000 lines. The saved log stops at 16 MiB, but the command continues and its final output tail and exit status remain visible in the preview. A “partial output” notice therefore does not mean the command was stopped or that the log contains its final lines. Nonzero exits, signals, and timeouts remain errors even when stdout exists. Timeout handling attempts to terminate the process tree, escalates termination, and bounds pipe drainage rather than waiting indefinitely for inherited pipes. Storage failure does not rerun a command. Commands are non-interactive: stdin is closed and there is no controlling terminal. Commands that need passwords, SSH prompts, or terminal interaction should be run in your own shell instead. On Unix, native, Seatbelt, and Bubblewrap shell runners own a process group. Failure, cancellation, timeout, buffered-output overflow, and orderly host exit trigger termination, with forced escalation if needed and bounded pipe drainage. Windows uses with forced escalation. This is best-effort cleanup, not rollback: descendants that escape the group and external side effects may remain. Under native and Seatbelt execution, successful background children are not killed merely because the shell leader finishes. Bubblewrap's private PID namespace and the Windows sandbox's Job Object prevent descendants from outliving the invocation. Output from children sharing the inherited pipes is collected until the pipes close or the command timeout bounds that wait. A successful leader can still be reported as successful when only pipe drainage reaches the timeout; do not interpret that status as proof that every background job completed. Manage persistent services explicitly, or use background jobs when a command must outlive the turn. The buffered runners used by some integrations still enforce their own output-buffer limits. shares the shell runner’s process-tree cleanup and bounded pipe drainage. Agent subprocesses do not inherit the shell runner’s process-group cleanup guarantees. MCP cancellation stops Agav's request wait without killing the shared server; server-side work may continue. Docker cancellation signals the local CLI but does not guarantee daemon/container cleanup. See Security. HTTP responses supports GET (default), HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE, with optional headers and body. It streams the response as decoded text, including raw HTML, with a 30-second request timeout. Once started, it does not consume the turn cancellation signal; Esc does not immediately stop that request or undo a POST or other server-side action. Small results include the HTTP status and body unchanged; above 38,000 decoded UTF-8 bytes, a response log and bounded head/tail preview are used. HEAD returns only status and rejects a request body. GET and HEAD are read-only for permission checks and run without a confirmation prompt. POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are blocked in and require explicit approval for each call in other modes, including . This requirement still applies if is allowlisted or you choose “always.” Agav refuses these methods when no confirmation handler is available. To protect against server-side request forgery (SSRF), accepts only HTTP(S) URLs and blocks loopback, private, link-local, reserved, and cloud metadata addresses. Agav rejects hostnames that resolve to any blocked address and pins each connection to a validated address. It applies the same destination checks to every redirect and follows at most five redirects. Cross-origin redirects strip , , and . See HTTP request safety. Unlike shell capture, HTTP capture cancels the remaining response when its 16 MiB incoming-byte or decoded-storage limit is exceeded. The notice marks the saved response as partial; the preview tail is from the captured prefix, not necessarily the end of the server's body. Reaching this size limit alone does not turn a successful HTTP status into an error. Non-success HTTP statuses and network/stream-read failures do remain errors, with the captured status/body retained where available. Log-storage failures do not repeat the request or change HTTP success status. The shared text limits and retention rules apply to these results too. Sandbox backends Each sandbox backend has different isolation properties: | Backend | Filesystem writes | Network | Credential dirs | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Seatbelt (macOS) | Denied by default; explicit workspace/temp/tooling allowances, with sensitive configuration protected | Allowed by default; opt-in deny | , , reads denied | | Bubblewrap (Linux) | Read-only root; private workspace snapshot with validated publication after successful, uncancelled execution; scratch temp/caches | Allowed by default; opt-in deny | , , masked | | Docker | Mounted working directory only | Denied () | Not mounted | | Windows restricted token | Workspace and dedicated temp; limitations apply | Not confined; refuses execution under | Reads not confined | When no backend is available, refuses shell and test execution. It defaults to on Windows and elsewhere; when disabled, automatic execution can run unsandboxed with secret-like environment variables (, , , …) filtered out. Only starting Agav with the user opt-out permits a model-requested override; command approval and auto-accept do not enable bypass. Invalid overrides are rejected, and sandbox launch failures are not retried unsandboxed. The footer describes the shell default; tool output identifies a different execution backend when an override is used. Review security before using auto-accept mode.

title: Detached sessions
content: Detached sessions Detach closes the terminal UI without cancelling the interactive task that its worker is executing. The worker keeps the conversation, model loop, and pending tool approvals alive on your machine. Return later with to see progress or answer an approval. This is different from simply saving a conversation: a saved transcript preserves history, while a detached session has a live process continuing the current turn. It is also different from a background job, which runs a shell command such as a dev server or watcher rather than an agent conversation. Enable before starting a task Merge this setting into , then start Agav: defaults to and is the only flag needed to enable worker-owned ordinary interactive turns and detaching. Enable it before submitting the task; does not migrate an already-running in-process turn into a worker. See Configuration for config precedence and Windows paths. With , ordinary interactive prompts start execution in a supervised worker after initial preparation, even while you are still watching the terminal. Detaching disconnects that presentation; it does not restart the task or run a second copy. Initial context and plan preparation happen before worker ownership is established. Ctrl+D works as soon as the worker is ready. When is enabled, randomized status-bar tips can include a detach hint using your configured shortcut; you do not need to wait for that hint. Detach and return 1. Start in your project and submit an ordinary task, for example: “Investigate the failing build and propose a fix.” 2. Once the worker is ready, type , or press Ctrl+D. Agav exits the UI and prints: 3. Keep that ID. From your shell, return with the printed command, replacing below with the actual ID: In Windows PowerShell, use the same command with the actual ID and no angle brackets: You can also run to open the picker at startup, or inside Agav. selects a session directly; ID prefixes are supported, but the full printed ID avoids choosing the wrong session. The detach shortcut works at a live worker’s approval prompt too. It leaves the request pending; it is not Yes, No, or Always. Use it when the confirmation owns input and you cannot type . The configurable action defaults to Ctrl+D. Ctrl+X cuts prompt text; it is not detach. Ctrl+Q is not detach: it opens the request queue when requests are queued, or exits while idle with an empty prompt. Detaching continues the current worker-owned turn, not an unattended stream of future chat requests. Unsent drafts and requests in the terminal queue are not handed off. The UI’s , , and triggers do not continue after it closes. Status and session management The resume picker includes live runtimes as well as saved conversations, even before their first completed-turn history save. Runtime rows display the state and pending approval count, for example . | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | | Worker execution is being established. | | | The worker is executing the turn. | | | One or more operations are waiting for your decision. | | | The turn finished. Resume to review it or submit another prompt. | | | Execution failed; resume to inspect the recorded conversation and error. | | | Execution ended without recording normal completion. | | | A terminal cancellation state, if present. | Select with ↑/↓, j/k, the mouse wheel, or a click; press Enter to resume. M or R renames both active and terminal sessions. Enter saves the new name; Esc cancels renaming. D deletes saved conversations and terminal runtimes only; deletion is unavailable for , , and sessions. Deleting history is not a way to stop a worker. Press or click the search bar to filter by session name, Tab to cycle project scope, s to toggle updated/created sorting, and a to cycle all/running/needs-approval filters. The running filter includes workers waiting for approval. An approval banner highlights sessions needing a decision. While search is focused, Enter or Esc leaves search editing without resuming or closing the picker. The worker checkpoints conversation progress and token usage, making recorded messages and usage visible when you resume, including through saved history. Live and saved session totals include subagent and skill usage. The UI observes those checkpoints rather than writing over the worker’s transcript. Successive ordinary turns keep the same session ID. A new turn has a new internal execution generation; you do not need to track that value or change the resume command. While the current worker is active, wait for completion or answer its approval rather than trying to start a competing turn in the same conversation. Approvals while detached In mode, an operation that needs confirmation waits for a durable approval. Closing the UI neither approves nor denies it. Resume the session, review the displayed tool name, inputs, diff, and warnings, and choose Yes or No in the confirmation UI. The live worker then continues the same pending invocation; it does not replay the task from the beginning. This applies to ordinary tools and to tools used by model-delegated subagents, skills, and service agents. Background-job actions requested by the model also keep their separate approval requirements. A detached session can therefore be alive but waiting rather than making progress. Detaching does not change the permission mode, widen tool access, or bypass an organization permission floor. remains restrictive; remains subject to policy. An Always choice cannot loosen an organization floor, and it does not turn the separate background-job policy into blanket consent. Explicit-approval-only operations still require explicit approval. Security and process lifetime - Local, not cloud execution. The worker runs as a local process under your OS account. Closing the Agav UI is supported; laptop sleep, logout, reboot, power loss, process cleanup, or losing provider/network access are not guarantees of continued execution. Suspension can pause work and disrupt connections. - Supervisor isolation is not tool isolation. The background-job supervisor launches the session worker outside the shell sandbox (). Inside the worker, tool execution still enforces its permission and sandbox requirements, including required-sandbox policy. Detaching is not a sandbox bypass. A shell command explicitly launched through is a separate, unsandboxed background job. - Credentials and overrides use a private launch path. Workers reload trusted configuration and selected provider environment variables. Registered / overrides also propagate through a private launch environment, using effective values so dedicated flags still take precedence. The override payload is not stored in command arguments or durable runtime metadata and is consumed before tools launch; organization policy still applies. Unregistered transient credential changes that differ from reloadable credentials remain refused. Stored endpoint choices cannot silently redirect current credentials after routing policy changes. - Durable state is not a replay engine. Runtime state, events, and approvals live under , with supervisor state under . A dead worker cannot resume its JavaScript promises. Agav does not automatically replay uncertain tool calls or restart that execution when you reopen the session. When a cancellation is pending and the owner is confirmed dead, Agav can mark the turn interrupted; it does not overwrite a recorded completion or assume death when owner identity cannot be verified. Supported paths and limitations Detaching is for worker-owned ordinary interactive turns. It is unavailable while disabled, before worker preparation finishes, or after the turn is terminal. Direct slash-command skill invocations and direct named/service-agent submissions use different execution paths and are not made detachable by this flag. This differs from a normal prompt whose model delegates to a skill, subagent, or service agent inside its worker. Steering is supported while attached to a live worker, including after resuming. Use to redirect the main agent at its next safe step within the same turn. In a live subagent inspector, it targets only that child; main-agent directives are not inherited by children. Worker delivery uses a durable inbox bound to the current execution and recipient, unlike the foreground in-memory directive list. Bare , , , and are unavailable while worker-attached or in a subagent inspector. See Planning and Steering. Pause remains unsupported for worker-owned turns. Foreground in-process turns retain pause controls. Steering does not interrupt an already-running tool or undo its effects. Use the documented and entry points to observe and answer a session. There is no separate public session , , , or command to substitute for this flow. To interrupt a worker, resume it and use the ordinary interrupt controls described below. Detach versus cancellation Only or the configured shortcut intentionally exits the UI while leaving the worker running. Ordinary and Ctrl+C exit request cancellation of the selected worker-owned turn; the cancel action (Esc by default) requests cancellation while keeping Agav open. Ctrl+C still copies an active Agav text selection instead of exiting. Esc can instead dismiss an overlay, deny a tool confirmation, or target a focused subagent; return to the overview to cancel the parent turn. The cancellation request is durable and bound to the current execution generation, so it cannot cancel a later turn in the same session. It is not synchronous termination: the worker must observe the request and settle its tools. Do not treat an exit, acknowledgement, or terminal status as proof that every process or external effect stopped. Already-applied edits are not rolled back; inspect the workspace and remote services before retrying. Switching sessions or unmounting the presentation only disconnects observation; neither requests cancellation nor answers pending approvals. These presentation changes are not substitutes for an explicit interrupt. If launch admission is uncertain (for example, a response was lost), Agav retains worker ownership fail-safe rather than starting a competing local loop. Resume to inspect the same execution; do not delete ownership records to force a retry. A definite launch failure is recorded as terminal and leaves the terminal UI usable for another prompt rather than permanently busy. Do and don't Do: - Enable and configure credentials before the task starts. - Detach once the worker is ready, save the exact resume command, and check the picker for pending approvals. - Review each approval and inspect the workspace before asking for follow-up work after an interruption. - Keep the machine awake, connected, and running if you need uninterrupted local execution. Don't: - Switch to merely to make detaching work; is supported. - Treat disconnecting, renaming, or deleting a session as approval or cancellation. - Delete runtime files, edit approval JSON, or kill supervisor/worker processes as a normal management workflow. That can destroy ownership evidence or interrupt work without knowing which side effects completed. - Assume sleep/reboot recovery will safely replay a partially executed tool call. Troubleshooting | Symptom | What to check | | --- | --- | | Detach is disabled | Set in global config, restart Agav, and start a new ordinary task. It cannot retrofit the current in-process execution. | | “The current task is not owned by a background worker yet” | Wait for worker preparation to finish; a status-bar hint is not required. If detaching remains unavailable, check whether you invoked a skill or service agent directly. | | “This session is no longer running” | The turn may have finished while you were detaching. Use or to inspect its terminal state. | | Session appears stuck | Look for and its pending count. Resume and explicitly approve or deny the displayed request. | | “Background execution cannot reload this transient credential override” | Use the matching provider environment variable, global config, or a registered credential override, then start a new task. Unregistered transient credential changes cannot be transferred. | | Worker failed or was interrupted | Resume to inspect the transcript/error and check the actual files or external effects before submitting follow-up instructions. Reopening observes recorded state; it does not resurrect a dead worker. | | “Session execution changed” or a stale approval error | Select the session again in to refresh its current execution and approval. Do not edit state files to force an old decision. | See Sessions and Memory for saved history, naming, and exports, and Background jobs for shell jobs and cron schedules.

title: Features
content: Features Agav combines a core toolset with extension points that add reusable knowledge and external capabilities. - Built-in tools cover files, search, shell, testing, language servers, notebooks, GitHub, web access, plans, and memory. - Voice input provides editable live English dictation with local recognition and an embedded native helper. - Skills package reusable instructions and tool policies, with a built-in marketplace, validation, and automatic improvement. - Detached sessions keep an interactive task running locally after you close its UI, with resumable progress and approvals. - Background jobs run long-lived commands and cron schedules that outlive a single turn. They are opt-in and unsandboxed. - MCP connects stdio subprocess servers and remote HTTP/SSE endpoints that expose tools, resources, and prompts. - Plugins and subagents add JavaScript tools and parallel task execution. - Agents are specialized sub-agents with scoped tools, credentials, and system prompts. - Agent Marketplace provides community-built agents for cloud platforms, developer workflows, and automation. Tools are chosen by the model based on the task. Read-only operations can run directly; sensitive operations follow the active permission mode and may require confirmation.

title: Model Context Protocol
content: Model Context Protocol Agav connects to MCP servers over two transport families: stdio (local subprocesses communicating through newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout) and remote (HTTP or SSE endpoints). Stdio servers Add to or : Each server supports a command, optional argument list, and optional environment overrides. Install the runner (such as Node.js/npm for ) and put it on the used to launch Agav. Stdio servers run outside the shell sandbox and inherit Agav’s launch environment, with configured values applied on top. Review project configs before starting Agav in unfamiliar checkouts. Restart Agav after changing server configuration. > Windows: resolves to . Agav uses for shim compatibility, regardless of your interactive shell. Keep and simple and separate; shell metacharacters and literal double quotes in either are rejected. On macOS and Linux arguments are passed directly, without a shell. See MCP command validation. Remote servers (HTTP / SSE) Remote servers connect to an MCP endpoint over the network instead of spawning a local process. Two transport modes are supported: - Streamable HTTP – the current MCP spec transport. Uses a single HTTP endpoint for both requests and server-initiated messages. - Legacy SSE – the older Server-Sent Events transport. Uses one SSE connection for server-to-client messages and a separate HTTP POST endpoint for client-to-server messages. When is omitted, Agav auto-detects: it tries Streamable HTTP first and falls back to Legacy SSE if the server does not support it. Basic configuration is optional when is present — Agav infers the server type automatically. Explicit transport selection If you know which transport the server speaks, pin it with : Remote server config fields | Field | Type | Required | Description | |-------|------|----------|-------------| | | string | yes | HTTP/SSE endpoint URL | | | | no | Explicitly marks the server as remote; inferred when is present | | | or | no | Force a specific transport; omit to auto-detect | | | Record\ | no | Extra headers sent with every request | are sent with every request and can pass static authentication tokens. Put real tokens in global config, not in a committed project file. Explicit headers take precedence over OAuth. The , , and fields are not used for remote servers. Limiting which tools are exposed Some MCP servers expose large tool catalogs, but a project may only need a few of them. Every exposed tool's schema is sent to the model on each request, so trimming an oversized catalog reduces the per-request tool overhead. Add an optional array to any server — stdio or remote — to expose only the listed tools. Names are written exactly as the server reports them (unprefixed, without the prefix Agav adds internally): Omit (or set it to an empty array) to expose every tool the server provides — the default. Selection is applied per server and preserves the server's own tool ordering, including after a live refresh. A configured name the server does not expose is reported on stderr and ignored, so a typo stays visible. If none of the configured names match, Agav warns and falls back to exposing all of that server's tools rather than silently disabling it. Restart Agav after changing the selection. Narrowing the exposed set is a context-size optimization, not a security boundary: MCP tools still require user confirmation under Agav's normal permission rules. OAuth authentication Agav discovers OAuth requirements when a remote MCP server returns a Bearer authentication challenge. Startup and tool requests never launch browser sign-in automatically. Cached tokens are reused or refreshed silently; servers needing sign-in are summarized in one startup warning. Run to view connected servers and those requiring authentication, then explicitly run to open your browser, complete the PKCE authorization flow, and connect that server without restarting. Other configured servers connect independently. For example, add Figma's remote server to : Figma remote access limitation: Figma currently rejects Agav's dynamic client registration with before browser sign-in. OAuth support alone does not bypass provider client restrictions. Remote access may require Figma to approve Agav; using another product's client identity is not a supported workaround. The remote configuration above shows the endpoint, but is not a verified working Agav/Figma integration. If your account supports Figma's desktop MCP server, enable it in the Figma desktop app and use its local endpoint instead: The desktop server has different availability and capabilities from the remote server. Keep Figma running and restart Agav after changing configuration. For servers that accept Agav's client registration, you can also sign in explicitly before starting Agav: Standalone CLI sign-in does not require an LLM provider. Restart Agav after using . In an existing Agav session, reconnects immediately; success feedback names the connected server and reports how many still require authentication. The startup warning updates as servers connect and disappears when none remain. Failed, denied, or canceled sign-in never reports success. If OAuth succeeds but MCP discovery fails, the error distinguishes those outcomes. Startup never launches a new browser login, whether interactive or not; it reuses cached credentials, refreshes tokens when possible, or reports the command needed to sign in. The sign-in timeout defaults to five minutes, separate from normal MCP request timeouts. Ctrl+C cancels standalone CLI sign-in; the normal interrupt/cancel shortcut cancels in-session sign-in. Duplicate sign-in requests for the same server are rejected while one is pending. OAuth tokens and registered client credentials are encrypted using Agav's existing local encryption utility and stored in private, atomically replaced files under , not in project configuration. This is local encryption, not an operating-system keychain. Cache entries are isolated by server name, URL, authentication settings, and configured headers. Treat this directory as sensitive. Expired tokens are refreshed automatically; revoked credentials may require sign-in again. To remove a server's cached credentials: Restart running Agav sessions after standalone CLI logout. In an existing session, run instead: it immediately disconnects that server, removes its tools/resources/prompt commands, cancels any pending sign-in, and deletes its cached OAuth credentials without restarting. Other servers stay connected. Run to sign in again. Logout removes local credentials; it does not revoke grants at the provider. Servers with an explicit header or cannot use in-session OAuth logout: remove their configured credentials instead. Stdio servers do not support OAuth logout. Optional remote-server configuration: | Field | Description | | --- | --- | | | Disable automatic OAuth for this server. | | | Use a pre-registered public client ID instead of dynamic registration. | | | Use and validate a specific authorization-server issuer. | | | Array of requested scopes. | | | Fixed loopback callback port; omitted or zero allocates and remembers a port. | | | Positive sign-in timeout; defaults to 300. | OAuth endpoints must use HTTPS, except for loopback development servers. Redirects and cross-origin MCP POST endpoints are rejected to avoid leaking credentials. Servers must support dynamic registration or a configured public client ID. Agav supports the authorization-code flow, not device-code or client-credentials grants. See Figma's remote MCP setup for Figma account and access requirements. Exposed capabilities - Tools are registered in the main tool pool with their server name prefixed to the tool name and shown in the description. MCP tools are not in the built-in safe list, so they require user confirmation before each call unless you are in mode or the tool is explicitly allowed via . - Resources are summarized in model context and read on demand through . - Prompts become slash commands. Agav requests the rendered prompt from the owning server and submits its messages to the conversation. If one server fails to start, Agav continues without it. Run to see connected servers or servers requiring sign-in, or for discovered resource and prompt counts. Completed MCP tool results in the interactive UI identify the server. Live refresh When a connected server sends , , or , Agav re-fetches the corresponding catalog from that server and updates the session immediately — no restart needed. This only applies to changes the server advertises at runtime; edits to itself still require a restart. Related - Research GitHub with an MCP Server — practical walkthrough using the GitHub MCP server

title: Plugins and Subagents
content: Plugins and Subagents Local plugins Agav loads and files from ( on Windows). A module can default-export one tool or export a array. Use for ES-module syntax on macOS, Linux, and Windows. Each tool needs , , , and an async function returning . The argument is an object with the properties defined in . Broken plugin modules are skipped. Modules are imported at startup, before any tool-call approval. Plugins run in-process, outside the shell sandbox, with the same access as Agav. Install only trusted code and restart Agav after changes. Parallel subagents The tool delegates a clear, self-contained task with a short UI title. Subagents: - have independent conversation context - inherit the active model, effort, system prompt, steers, permission mode, and available tools - can optionally run on a different model (see below) - cannot create nested subagents - share confirmations through the main terminal UI - report streaming progress and token usage - allow up to five concurrent tasks Running a subagent on a different model A subagent accepts an optional parameter. Omit it to use the active session model — the default. Set it only when you explicitly want a specific model for the delegated task; the requested model must exist and is subject to explicit per-call user approval. The requested model must also satisfy any organization policy that applies to the parent session (a managed model pin or allowlist), so a subagent cannot route inference around the policy through a different model or provider. While subagents run, the terminal shows a live overview. Use / to select a subagent and to inspect it. Press the cancel key ( by default) to cancel just the focused subagent while inspecting it, or to cancel all running subagents from the overview. See Keybindings for the subagent navigation shortcuts. Tasks whose description indicates file changes attempt to use an isolated Git worktree. On successful completion, Agav commits remaining tracked edits and non-ignored new files, then merges the complete worker branch back into the original checkout. Worker directory and branch names include a unique suffix so retained work does not collide with workers in later sessions. If Git cannot create the worktree, the task stops with an error instead of running in the parent checkout. Read-only tasks and tasks outside Git repositories use the current working directory directly. Worktree delivery and recovery Agav records the Git commit where each worker started. Delivery uses a normal merge commit, preserving all worker commits since that base along with any final uncommitted edits. An unchanged worker is a no-op; ignored files are excluded unless the worker explicitly tracks them. Both the parent and worker histories must still descend from the recorded base. Automatic integration requires a clean parent index and tracked working files, with no merge, rebase, or cherry-pick in progress. Parent commits made while the worker runs are preserved. Agav previews the merge before modifying the parent, including directory-rename destinations, and checks local untracked and ignored files for collisions using filesystem identity. This also protects case-equivalent file and directory names on case-insensitive volumes. Automatic integration ignores for its Git commands so preview and execution agree; the saved repository configuration is unchanged. Install Git on the used to launch Agav. On Windows, model-invoked Git commands in a linked worktree can fail if the restricted-token shell sandbox blocks writes to repository metadata outside that worktree. Agav’s own delivery uses Git directly, not the model’s shell tool. Automatic integration requires Git with support; if the preview is unavailable or conflicts, work is retained for manual integration. If staging, committing, or merging fails, the tool reports an error and retains the worker directory and branch. The error includes both names so you can inspect the output, resolve conflicts, or integrate it manually. For example, using the actual path and branch from the error: Failed automatic merges are aborted. If Git cannot abort or roll back, the error also asks you to inspect the parent repository. Successful delivery removes only that worker's directory and branch. Cancellation discards worker output; if it arrives during integration, Agav rolls the merge back before cleanup. Once delivery has completed, cancellation does not undo it. Give a subagent all necessary paths, constraints, and expected output because it is instructed to work without follow-up questions. Related - Create a Local Plugin — step-by-step plugin authoring guide - Coordinate Parallel Subagents — patterns for splitting work across subagents

title: Skills
content: Skills Skills are reusable instruction packages that extend Agav with domain-specific procedures. Each skill is a file — YAML front-matter declaring metadata, followed by a Markdown body containing the instructions the LLM follows when the skill is activated. Skills let you encode repeatable workflows (code review, test generation, research) and share them across projects and teams. Loading order Skills are loaded from three tiers. A skill in a later tier with the same slug replaces the earlier definition: | Tier | Location | Override priority | |------|----------|-------------------| | Bundled | Shipped with Agav binary | Lowest | | Global | | Middle | | Project | in the working directory | Highest | > Windows: paths resolve to . When a project skill overrides a bundled or global skill, the override is tracked and shown as in and . If two skills in the same tier share a slug, the second is skipped with a warning. Skills whose slug collides with a built-in command name (e.g. , , ) are also silently skipped. Bundled skills are compiled directly into the binary, so they work even when running from a compiled build where file system paths are unavailable. Bundled skills Agav ships with 21 bundled skills. They are disabled by default — each is compiled into the binary but opt-in, so none are offered to the model or exposed as a slash command until you enable it with (see Enabling bundled skills). Global and project skills remain enabled by default. | Skill | Description | Invocation | |-------|-------------|------------| | | Review code changes for bugs, security issues, and improvements | auto + manual | | | Clean up and analyze CSV/Excel data for non-analysts | auto + manual | | | Multi-source research on a topic with citations | manual | | | Diagnose and fix errors and bugs | auto + manual | | | Generate documentation for code | auto + manual | | | Create, read, edit, and review Word .docx documents | auto + manual | | | Draft emails and replies with the right tone — never sends them | auto + manual | | | Explain code in plain language | auto + manual | | | Clean up a messy folder with a dry-run plan before moving anything | auto + manual | | | Generate a commit message from staged changes | auto + manual | | | Turn raw meeting notes or transcripts into structured minutes | auto + manual | | | Extract text from, merge, split, and fill PDF files | auto + manual | | | Rewrite text to be clear and understandable for any reader | auto + manual | | | Create and edit PowerPoint .pptx presentations | auto + manual | | | Suggest and apply code refactoring | auto + manual | | | Check code for security vulnerabilities | manual | | | Reduce complexity and simplify code | auto + manual | | | Guide for authoring a new agav skill (SKILL.md) | manual | | | Summarize documents, web pages, or pasted text at any depth | auto + manual | | | Generate unit tests for existing code | auto + manual | | | Create, read, and edit Excel .xlsx spreadsheets and CSV files | auto + manual | Using skills Skills can be invoked in two ways depending on their setting: - * — called explicitly as a slash command: - — selected automatically by the LLM when a query matches the skill's triggers - — available both ways Watch a running skill Skills activated through appear in the live subagent overview as Skill: , including when you invoke a skill such as . While the main turn is running, use ↑ / ↓ to select the skill, Enter to inspect it, and Tab to return to the overview. Manual-only () skills such as display their detail panel directly while running; you do not need to press Enter. Before the first activity event, this path shows a “Running skill” spinner. The detail panel shows the task, reasoning summary when the provider emits one, streaming text, and Recent actions (up to 10). Recent actions retain tool inputs, statuses, and available edit diffs across model messages — they do not disappear just because the model starts its next response. This is a recent-activity view, not a complete tool log. The session footer includes skill token usage as provider usage events arrive: ↑ input, ↓ output, ⇢ cache reads, and ⇠ cache writes when present. Completion does not add the skill total a second time. Usage already reported is retained after failure or cancellation; emitted or thrown errors record an unsuccessful trace, but interruption alone does not guarantee that trace status. Unreported provider usage cannot be counted. Tool-activated skill entries share the worker UI but do not support focused Esc cancellation. Return to the overview with Tab, then press Esc to cancel their parent turn. Individual focused cancellation applies only to actual workers. Manual-only slash-command skills currently receive no turn cancellation signal; their progress panel does not make Esc a reliable way to stop them. Permissions still apply A live progress panel does not approve actions. Tool-activated skills inherit the session's permission mode and route sensitive-action approvals to the main terminal. Review the tool input and available diff before approving; continues to block designated file-mutating/destructive tools, but is not a universal read-only or network-side-effect boundary. Manual-only slash-command skills currently run without an interactive confirmation handler. In mode, operations requiring confirmation are refused and fenced shell blocks are skipped rather than approved silently. Use a read-only task in this mode; do not switch to merely to bypass a refusal. See Security for permission modes and Shell blocks for their specific behavior. Automatic dispatch When a user message starts with , Agav immediately activates that skill without planning. This is used internally by the LLM for automatic skill selection. Dynamic context variables Skill bodies support two placeholder variables that are replaced at runtime: - — replaced with the user's arguments, or if none - — replaced with the current working directory Steer integration Active directives from are appended to the skill's system prompt, so user guidance applies even inside skill execution. Installing skills From a local file or directory When pointing to a directory, Agav copies the entire tree (excluding , , , and ). When pointing to a bare SKILL.md file, it copies the file plus sibling asset directories (, , ) if present. Batch install: If the target directory contains no at the root but has subdirectories with files, all subdirectories are installed independently. Failures in one skill don't block others. Size limits: Installations are capped at 200 files and 10 MB total. Exceeding either limit is refused before any files are copied. From a URL Agav normalizes common GitHub URL formats automatically: - → raw content URL - → raw content URL with appended - Bare repo URL → appends If the URL returns an HTML page instead of Markdown, Agav reports a clear error rather than a confusing validation failure. GitHub batch install: If a single URL 404s, Agav checks whether the URL points to a directory containing multiple skill subdirectories and installs all of them. From the marketplace The marketplace opens an interactive TUI with two tabs — Marketplace (browse and install) and Installed (manage what you already have): - Tab to switch between the Marketplace and Installed tabs - ↑↓ to navigate, ←→ to page (5 skills per page) - s to search by name or description - ENTER to install the selected marketplace skill - In the Installed tab, d (or ENTER) toggles a skill between enabled and disabled — this works on bundled skills too - r to refresh the catalog - ESC to exit Already-installed skills show a badge and cannot be reinstalled. In the Installed tab each skill shows its origin and an / state. Removing skills Only global (user-installed) skills can be removed. Bundled skills live inside the binary and project skills belong to the repo, so on one of those reports an error and points you to instead. Removing a global skill also clears any disabled state it had, so reinstalling it later starts enabled again. Restart Agav after installing or removing a skill. Enabling bundled skills Bundled skills ship disabled by default, so you opt into the ones you want: A disabled skill is excluded from the catalog the model sees, has no slash command, and cannot be activated — but it still appears in marked so you can enable it. Enabling one records an explicit opt-in; the choice is stored in and survives upgrades. Restart Agav after enabling or disabling a skill. Global and project skills behave the opposite way: they are enabled by default and turns them off. Bundled skills are compiled into the binary, so they cannot be removed with or — disable them instead.
