title: Voice Input
content: Voice Input Run in an idle interactive Agav session to speak instead of typing. Agav's native voice helper captures microphone audio and runs English-only Whisper locally. No FFmpeg, whisper-cli, Python, package manager, sudo, or PATH changes are required. Browser speech APIs and cloud transcription are not used. Interactive setup The native helper is embedded inside the Agav executable, compressed as a bundled asset. On first use Agav verifies and extracts it to a private executable cache under . Cached bytes are reverified, and corrupt files are replaced from the embedded payload without network access. License files are extracted alongside it. Only the English model needs a download. If missing, shows Whisper base.en Q5, its pinned Hugging Face URL and exact size 59,721,011 bytes (59.7 MB). Press Y or click Y download to approve; N, Esc, or Ctrl+C declines. Enter alone does not consent. Progress and cancellation are supported; size/SHA-256 checks and atomic publication protect installation. Downloads have a ten-minute timeout. The model is saved at and reused across sessions/versions. After setup, the current voice request continues into recording. There is no helper metadata request, helper download, or separately published helper asset. > Windows: paths resolve to . Developer builds: normal , tests, typecheck and do not compile native voice code or require CMake/C++. Use * or to explicitly compile and embed voice. A prebuilt helper can be supplied with , but is only used with . Release CI always builds/embeds voice and fails if it cannot do so. means all targets and all features, including voice. Supply prebuilt helpers for all five native targets in (, , , , ). Both Windows variants reuse the Windows x64 helper. Missing helpers fail before compilation rather than silently omitting voice. CI obtains helpers on native runners. enables every optional feature for the current native target; enables only voice. Future optional features belong in the central all-feature selection. Plain source/default builds have no embedded helper; requires a local helper override or a voice-enabled build. Build scripts restore the source stub on exit so generated payloads are not committed. Advanced local overrides | Environment variable | Purpose | | --- | --- | | | Existing English-only whisper.cpp GGML model, readable regular file between 1 MiB and 4 GiB. Leading is expanded. | | | Existing protocol-1 Agav native helper executable. Windows requires a native or , not a shell/batch wrapper. | | | Optional exact microphone name; omitted uses the system default on every platform, including Windows. Ambiguous/missing names produce an error. | Invalid explicit overrides produce errors rather than silently replacing them. Unset overrides to use the embedded helper and managed model. and are no longer used. Language settings are not configurable. Examples for a development checkout (use an absolute path to your helper and model): macOS / Linux: Windows PowerShell: The helper links pinned whisper.cpp and miniaudio versions. See for its CMake build, model-free self-test, protocol tests, licenses, and optional microphone-free WAV validation. Build tooling is for maintainers only, not end-user setup. Native build artifacts belong outside the source tree. Microphone and platform support The helper supports macOS ARM64/x64, Linux ARM64/x64, and Windows x64. There is no native Windows ARM64 helper: Windows ARM64 uses x64 Agav and its x64 helper under emulation. The helper uses system audio backends through miniaudio: Core Audio, WASAPI, and available Linux audio services such as PulseAudio/ALSA. No audio server SDK is required by the client, but a working host audio device/service must exist. - macOS: allow microphone access for your terminal/helper in Privacy & Security → Microphone. The helper embeds a microphone-purpose description. - Windows: allow desktop-app microphone access in privacy settings. The default microphone requires no device configuration. - Linux: ensure your audio service/device is available to the current user. - SSH, WSL, containers: capture uses the audio devices visible to the Agav process. Agav does not forward the microphone from your client machine or from Windows into WSL. English-only recording and review 1. Remove pending attachments and run while idle. 2. Complete setup if prompted, then wait for Listening. The meter reflects real audio and shows elapsed time. Partial English transcripts appear live while speaking; the current draft can revise itself as more audio arrives. 3. New speech appears directly in the visible composer. You can type, delete and move the caret while recognition continues; incoming updates preserve your edits and do not send anything automatically. 4. Press Enter once to send the exact displayed draft after microphone cleanup; late recognition revisions do not alter what you chose to send. 5. Alternatively, click Stop to finish without sending, reconcile the final recognition result, then edit and submit normally. Recording is limited to two minutes. The helper fixes recognition to English, keeps base.en Q5 (no tiny fallback), disables language detection/translation, and rejects multilingual model files. The default download is Whisper's variant. Recognized slash commands and shell text are never executed automatically. Esc, Ctrl+C, or clicking Cancel discards recording or transcription. Keyboard release/repeat events are ignored by voice controls. Scheduled work is deferred during dictation; automated requests cannot open the microphone. Typed input remains the fallback after errors. Live recognition uses a background worker with start-to-start one-second scheduling and bounded five-second, pause-aware audio chunks, not a new pass over the whole recording for every update. Actual update latency depends on hardware/inference time and is not a guaranteed one-second response. Words at chunk boundaries may be misrecognized; review the final draft. Live text appears directly in the prompt. The composer remains editable during capture and finalization. Enter/Escape stay owned by voice controls; typing, deletion and navigation stay owned by the editor. Accepted speech is retained when recognition backtracks or returns an empty/shorter draft; matching cumulative extensions append new trailing words without replaying user-deleted words. Related recognition corrections rebase the speech comparison without replacing your visible wording, so later words can continue arriving. Unrelated rewrites are ignored rather than destructively replacing your draft. This favors stability over automatically correcting earlier recognition errors. Escape cancels a pending Enter send; helper failures preserve the draft and never send it. The ready hint disappears as soon as you edit. Known Whisper annotations such as , and may remain visible during recording. They are removed when recording ends, when you click Stop, or when you press Enter. The sent snapshot and final recognition are cleaned; annotation-only drafts are never sent to the LLM. Ordinary informational bracketed/code text is not stripped indiscriminately. Privacy and failure handling The helper holds audio in a fixed, bounded memory buffer. Background inference runs during capture, and the microphone is released before final reconciliation/ready acknowledgment. Normal recording does not write WAV or transcript files. No raw audio is added to history or uploaded. The consented model download is setup traffic, not remote recognition; the helper is extracted locally without a download. Local recognition does not make the conversation offline: explicitly submitted transcript text uses your configured LLM provider and normal session history. Missing developer bundles, invalid English models/devices, permissions, silence, malformed helper events, protocol mismatch and timeouts produce visible diagnostics. Silence rejection is an energy guard, not neural VAD; recognition may still mishear background noise, so review drafts. The parent owns the helper through protocol probing, capture and inference. Cancellation first requests cooperative shutdown, then escalates termination. If termination is not acknowledged, Agav reports uncertainty instead of claiming microphone release. Prefer direct helper binaries, not wrappers spawning descendants. Unavailable model filesystems or OS initialization calls can delay native shutdown until the parent deadline. Performance controls Agav retains the helper/model context for up to 30 seconds between recordings, while the microphone is closed whenever the helper acknowledges ready. Each start gets a fresh audio buffer and transcript state. Changing model/helper/device/thread/backend settings retires the old pool. UI teardown disposes it; the native process also exits after a 60-second idle limit. - macOS: Metal with embedded shaders and Accelerate are built by default. Failed GPU initialization/inference can retry CPU; driver hangs still require parent deadlines. forces CPU; is the default. - Windows/Linux/macOS x64: the embedded baseline safely probes CPUID and OS AVX state before selecting a separately embedded AVX2/FMA/F16C helper. Unsupported CPUs use the baseline, never speculative AVX2 execution. forces baseline. Prebuilt build overrides include an optional sibling; without it they remain baseline-only. - Threads: overrides the default bounded four-thread setting. More threads are not always faster; benchmark representative hardware. - Profiling:** emits timing JSON on stderr, without changing transcript stdout events or uploading audio. The worker reuses a reserved decode buffer, skips silence-only/unchanged work conservatively, and commits at quiet tails or the five-second limit. It does not claim true incremental encoder caching. No ONNX dependency or smaller model is introduced. For a microphone-free cold-process real-time replay benchmark: Compare on macOS. Output records first partial/final timings and native inference/sample-position telemetry. Native profiling includes accumulated CPU milliseconds and peak resident/working-set bytes (GPU memory is not included); missing resource telemetry is reported as unavailable. The replay script does not label fresh-process replay as warm-session benchmarking. Validation status Automated coverage includes protocol parsing, stream/output limits, cancellation/escalation, dependency probing, download size/hash verification, atomic installation, consent, stale results, mouse/keyboard controls, and English-only model selection. Native macOS ARM64 builds pass model-free self-tests and microphone-free protocol tests; x64 cross-compilation was checked separately. Native release jobs build, test and embed the matching helper into each main Agav binary. Real microphone permissions/device behavior on every OS, actual coding-dictation accuracy, peak inference memory and latency remain release validation requirements. No real audio/model inference was performed during the model-free tests. Helper extraction works entirely offline from a correctly bundled binary; only initial model setup needs internet.

title: Getting Started
content: Getting Started This path takes you from installation to a safe first change in an existing repository. Before you begin You need: - a terminal on a supported platform: macOS, Linux, or Windows - a local Git repository to explore - an API key for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, NVIDIA NIM, or DeepSeek; a Google Cloud service-account JSON file for Vertex AI; or a running local server such as Ollama, llama.cpp, or LM Studio The prebuilt Agav release does not require Node.js. Node.js and pnpm are only needed when developing Agav itself. Follow this path 1. Install Agav and verify that the command works. 2. Connect a provider so Agav can use a model. 3. Complete your first task in a real repository, beginning with tool writes restricted. 4. Configure your project with shared instructions and defaults when you are ready. At the end, you will know how to open the correct workspace, give Agav exact context, review a proposed change, and check what changed. If you are already set up, go directly to the first-task walkthrough.

Pre-release builds Betas ship as GitHub pre-releases. asks the installer for the newest entry returned by the GitHub releases list, which includes both stable and pre-release builds. title: Run Local Models
content: Run Local Models Agav can use a local inference server that exposes an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. Agav sends requests to the server; it does not load model files itself. selects the API format, not the host. When the effective endpoint is on , model requests go to your local server rather than OpenAI. Before using the environment examples below, check for a saved or a managed gateway that takes precedence over . | What you want to run | Server | Base URL in these examples | | --- | --- | --- | | A GGUF model from the command line | from llama.cpp | | | A GGUF model in a desktop app | LM Studio | | | An MLX model on Apple Silicon | LM Studio with its MLX runtime | | Use the Ollama provider instead if you already run Ollama. There are no separate Agav provider flags for llama.cpp, LM Studio, or MLX. Serve a GGUF model with llama.cpp Install llama.cpp and download an instruction-tuned GGUF model that fits your machine. In one terminal, replace the model path and start llama-server: Leave the server running. In a second terminal, confirm that it lists , then start Agav from your repository: sets the model ID used by the API. If you use a different alias or omit it, copy the from the response into . Serve a GGUF or MLX model with LM Studio 1. Install LM Studio, download an instruction-tuned model, and load it. For MLX on an Apple Silicon Mac, choose the MLX version of the model, not the GGUF version. LM Studio runs the MLX runtime; the Agav settings are the same for both formats. 2. Open LM Studio's Developer tab and start the local server. Keep Serve on Local Network off for use on the same machine. The default port is ; use the port shown in LM Studio if yours differs. 3. Copy the loaded model's API identifier from LM Studio or find its in the model list. Replace with that exact identifier: In Windows PowerShell, set the environment variables before launching Agav. To start llama.cpp, use the same server command with your Windows model path (for example ), and use port and model ID below. This example uses LM Studio: Authentication and saved defaults Agav's provider requires a nonempty key. Use only as a placeholder when your loopback server does not require authentication. If you enabled authentication, set to the server's actual token and include on manual requests. Do not send your OpenAI cloud key to a local server. Keep an unauthenticated server bound to loopback. To make local inference the default, merge these fields into your user config ( on macOS/Linux or on Windows). The example uses llama.cpp; substitute the LM Studio URL and model ID if needed: Continue to supply when you start Agav, or set in your user config. Keep credentials and endpoint overrides out of the repository's . The inline macOS/Linux assignments apply only to that launch; PowerShell assignments persist in the current terminal. Before switching back to hosted OpenAI, use a fresh terminal or remove and with and set your hosted credentials. If you also use hosted OpenAI, prefer the per-launch examples; a saved applies to all requests made through the provider, not just one model. Verify chat and tool calls First ask Agav to respond with without using tools. Then ask it to list a few files in your repository without editing anything. Check that Agav shows an actual tool call, not merely a plausible answer. Basic chat working does not guarantee tool use: the server must return structured tool calls, and the model and its chat template must support them. See llama.cpp function calling and LM Studio tool use. Troubleshooting | Symptom | What to check | | --- | --- | | Connection refused | Keep the inference server running, confirm the host and port, and try the command from the same machine as Agav. | | HTTP 404 or unknown model | Set the base URL to the server's root, not or LM Studio's . Use and the exact model ID returned by the server. | | Missing OpenAI API key or HTTP 401 | Set a nonempty in the terminal that launches Agav. If the server requires auth, use its token instead of . | | Requests reach a different server | Check your saved and any organization-managed gateway. An explicit base URL takes precedence over the SDK's fallback, and a managed gateway can pin the endpoint. | | Chat works but tools don't | Try a model advertised for tool calling and its matching chat template. For llama.cpp, check that Jinja templates are enabled () and that the template supports tools. | | Context errors or the server runs out of memory | Check the server logs and its configured context size. title: Configure a Project
content: Configure a Project You can use Agav without project configuration. Add it when a repository has conventions that Agav should follow consistently. Start at the project root Agav treats the current directory as its workspace. Start from the repository root so file suggestions and tools can reach the whole project: paths are relative to this directory and cannot escape it through or symlinks. Add repository instructions Create or at the project root. Agav tries first and falls back to if needed. Write short, actionable rules that apply across tasks. Put the details of a one-time task in its prompt instead. User-level instructions Create ( on Windows) for instructions that apply to every project. When both a user-level and a project / exist, Agav loads both, with the user-level instructions first followed by the project instructions. Use the user-level file for personal conventions (preferred tools, response style) and the project file for repository-specific rules. Save project defaults Project settings live in and override global defaults from ( on Windows). Agav creates or enriches the project file without overwriting values already there. is a global-only setting — set it in or use / at startup. It cannot be set in project configuration to prevent untrusted repositories from silently escalating permissions. MCP servers can be declared in project config so every session in the repository gets the same tools: Do not commit API keys. Use provider environment variables or secure user-level configuration for credentials. See the configuration reference for every field and the full precedence rules. API keys, endpoint overrides, and cannot be set from project config at all — Agav strips them before use — so those fields in a committed are not used. That does not make project config safe to trust: it can still declare MCP servers that launch local commands. Review unfamiliar project configuration before starting Agav. This protection comes from that deny-list, not from gitignore: ignoring only guards against committing your own config by accident, and a cloned repo can ship a regardless (even overrides ). See project config restrictions for details. Know what is shared | Item | Scope | | --- | --- | | or | Repository instructions | | | User-level instructions, applied to every project (loaded before project instructions) | | | Project defaults (provider, model, , …) | | | Defaults for your user account | | | Reusable skill overrides for this project | | | Project-local agents | | , , and | User-level extensions | | | Per-project memory, auto-saved across sessions | | | Saved interactive sessions | > Windows: paths resolve to (e.g. ). Agav also ships with built-in skills (like , , ) that are disabled by default. Enable the ones you want with . Project and user skills can override a built-in skill of the same name. Per-project memory is keyed by a hash of the Git root path (or the working directory outside Git), so Agav remembers context about each repository without storing anything inside the repo itself. See sessions and memory for details. You have completed the beginner path. Continue with daily workflows or use the task finder.

title: Connect a Provider
content: Connect a Provider Agav needs one model provider. The easiest path is: 1. choose one provider 2. set its credential in the same terminal where you will start Agav 3. launch Agav with that provider and model 4. ask one read-only question to confirm it works Anthropic is the default provider, with on a fresh 0.2.9 configuration. If that provider is not configured, plain can select another configured cloud provider. Use for a local Ollama server; it is not discovered as a fallback. If you are not sure which provider to pick, use OpenAI, Anthropic, or Gemini if you already have an API key. Use OpenRouter if you want access to multiple providers behind a single key. Use NVIDIA NIM for NVIDIA-hosted models. Use DeepSeek for DeepSeek's own models. Use Ollama if you already have it installed, or run a local model through an OpenAI-compatible server with llama.cpp or LM Studio. Use Vertex AI if you already run on Google Cloud and want Gemini or Claude billed through that project. Fastest path If you already have an OpenAI key, this is the quickest first run: In Windows PowerShell: Use the same pattern for other providers ( in Command Prompt). These assignments affect the current shell and processes launched from it. Then ask: OpenAI By default Agav uses the OpenAI Responses API. If you need the Chat Completions API instead (for example behind a proxy that only supports it), pass : Custom base URL (OpenAI-compatible endpoints) Many services speak the OpenAI API without being OpenAI — private gateways, self-hosted deployments, LiteLLM/vLLM servers, or vendors that expose an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Point the provider at one with instead of adding a dedicated provider: Or set it in : The base URL applies only to the provider. An explicit takes precedence over the SDK's fallback. If neither is set and no managed gateway applies, requests go to OpenAI. Most OpenAI-compatible endpoints implement Chat Completions rather than the Responses API, so pair a custom base URL with if requests fail. For step-by-step examples with GGUF models in llama.cpp and GGUF or MLX models in LM Studio, see Run Local Models. If your gateway needs extra HTTP headers — a custom auth header, a tenant selector, or routing metadata — set in . They are sent with OpenAI-provider requests. Custom headers are not the encrypted API-key fields, so protect the user config if you put a token there: OpenRouter OpenRouter aggregates multiple model providers behind a single API key. Set the key as an environment variable: Start Agav with OpenRouter: The default model is , which lets OpenRouter choose the best model for each request. You can also specify any model available on OpenRouter: Or set it in : and switch models — see the table below for every provider's mapping. NVIDIA NIM NVIDIA NIM provides access to NVIDIA-hosted models through an OpenAI-compatible API. Set the API key: Start Agav with NVIDIA NIM: The default model is . All models use the prefix: Or set it in : Context window sizes are detected automatically from the NVIDIA API. The API base URL is . DeepSeek DeepSeek provides access to DeepSeek's own models through an OpenAI-compatible API. Set the API key: Start Agav with DeepSeek: The default model is . DeepSeek also offers for faster, lighter responses: Or set it in : Context window sizes are detected automatically from the DeepSeek API. The API base URL is . Anthropic Google Gemini Vertex AI Vertex AI authenticates with a Google Cloud service-account JSON file rather than an API key. Point Agav at the file, then select the provider: On Windows PowerShell, use an absolute path and quote it, for example . Setting the credentials path is what enables the provider; there is no separate on/off flag to keep in sync with it. Agav uses the multi-region endpoint by default — set (for example ) to pin a region instead, which some Claude partner models require. Claude partner models are supported by the same provider and credentials, addressed with the same prefix. Use the model ID that Vertex AI exposes, including an suffix when required by that model: Vertex AI selects , which requires (or ) to be , , or . With a regional location such as , rejects the switch without changing your model or location. Configure a supported location explicitly, or use to choose a regional model. title: Your First Repository Task
content: Your First Repository Task This walkthrough uses prapaa-ai/hello-agav, a tiny Python CLI that greets you and counts its own runs. It is small enough to explore in five minutes and has one obvious thing to improve. You can use the same prompts in your own repository. 1. Open the repository root These commands also work in PowerShell. Start Agav from the directory that contains the whole project. Agav treats that folder as the project root, so it uses it to decide which files it can see, which project settings to load, and which suggestions to offer. 2. Start read-only mode lets Agav inspect the repository while blocking write and approval-required tools. It is a tool permission mode, not an operating-system sandbox. Replace the provider and model if you configured a different one. The interactive session opens with a compact shell logo (braille on macOS/Linux, block characters on Windows), , and Stay in the Shell. The name and tagline sit beside the logo on wider terminals and stack below it on narrow ones. The footer shows your provider, model, effort, and session token usage; the logo is a static banner, not a new thinking animation. 3. Ask a focused first question Paste this prompt: Typing opens file suggestions. Choose a path with Up or Down, then press Enter or Tab to attach it. An attachment gives Agav exact context; the question tells it what to do with that context. For this repository, the answer should identify as the entry point and explain how it calls to build the message and to track runs via . 4. Narrow the investigation Follow the broad tour with one concrete path through the code: Focused follow-ups are easier to verify than repeatedly asking for a complete repository summary. If Agav activates a skill or delegates work to subagents, their live progress appears below the transcript. While the main turn is running, use ↑ / ↓ to select a worker, Enter to inspect its task and recent tool actions, and Tab to return to the overview. Manual-only skills show their detail panel directly. See Skills and Coordinate Parallel Subagents for the differences. Markdown links in terminal replies display as , with a bare URL shown only once. Long URLs wrap with the terminal width, and detected URL fragments remain clickable across wrapped lines. Click the visible URL to open it in a browser where one is available. On a remote or headless terminal, copy the URL into your local browser if opening it is unavailable; see Troubleshooting. Terminal replies also render a supported subset of LaTeX math as Unicode: for example, becomes . Inline and , and display and , support common Greek letters, operators, fractions, roots, and superscripts/subscripts. This is not full LaTeX typesetting: unsupported formulas remain literal, and code spans, code blocks, and link destinations are left unchanged. 5. Make one controlled change Exit Agav, then start a new session without (resuming can keep the previous session's permission mode): Ask for a small change with a clear boundary: Check and choose if your settings use a different mode. pauses before sensitive actions and shows edit diffs. Check the file path and proposed change before approving. Reject the action and clarify your request if it is broader than expected. 6. Review the result After Agav finishes, review the repository yourself: These commands distinguish Agav's work from changes that already existed. Use and to revert a specific Agav file change, or use your normal Git workflow afterward. Tips for longer sessions - Use to reclaim context if the conversation gets long — it summarises history without starting over. - Use to revert the last file edit without leaving Agav. - Resume a past session with instead of starting from scratch. What you learned You now know the core Agav loop: 1. open the repository root 2. begin read-only when learning unfamiliar code 3. attach exact context and ask a specific question 4. narrow the scope before requesting a change 5. review confirmations, diffs, and Git state For scripting and CI, see non-interactive mode — and let you use the same agent from pipelines and automation. Next: add project instructions and defaults, or learn more about files and context.

title: Compose Agents, Skills, and Tools
content: Compose Agents, Skills, and Tools Combine capabilities when one task has reusable rules, quick local checks, and independent investigations. Scenario: review a counter.py change A change to can affect how calls it, what contains, and whether tests still pass. This division keeps responsibilities clear: | Layer | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Skill | Repeatable module-review procedure | | Main prompt | This change, its paths, and the required report | | Direct tools | Small checks needed in the main conversation | | Subagents | Independent downstream investigations | Ask the main agent to reconcile the results before starting an implementation phase. Keep temporary repository paths in the prompt, not in a global skill. Expected result You get one review that covers the counter module and every downstream consumer without making each worker inspect the whole repository. Next: Automate with Loops, Watch, and Schedules.

title: Create an Agent with the Wizard
content: Create an Agent with the Wizard The agent creation wizard lets you build a custom agent in five guided steps — name it, generate a system prompt with your LLM, select built-in native tools, attach MCP servers, and save. Agav writes the manifest for you and registers the agent immediately. This guide walks through creating a agent from scratch, then covers editing existing agents and working with templates. Prerequisites - Agav installed and connected to an LLM provider (needed for automatic system prompt generation) Step 1: Open the Create tab Start Agav and type: Press to switch to the Create tab. This is the "My Agents" hub — it shows your user-created agents, saved templates, and a button at the top. If you haven't created any agents yet, the list will be empty except for the entry. Step 2: Start the wizard Navigate to and press to launch the five-step creation wizard. A progress bar at the top tracks your position through the flow: You can press or at any step to go back to the previous one without losing your input. Step 3: Name and describe the agent The first step asks for two fields: Name and Description. Name — type a short, unique identifier for your agent. Names must be lowercase alphanumeric characters, hyphens, dots, or underscores, with a maximum length of 64 characters. For example: Press or to move to the Description field. Description — write a one-line summary of what the agent does. This appears in the agent list and helps the LLM understand when to route queries to this agent: Press to advance to the next step. Step 4: Review the system prompt Agav sends your name and description to your configured LLM provider and auto-generates a system prompt tailored to the agent's purpose. The prompt streams in real-time inside a bordered preview box. Once generation completes, review the prompt. It typically includes: - A role definition ("You are a GitHub assistant…") - Guidelines for tool usage - Response formatting instructions If the prompt doesn't match what you need, press to regenerate it. You can regenerate as many times as you like — each attempt produces a fresh prompt based on your name and description. When you're satisfied, press to accept the prompt and continue. Step 5: Select native tools (optional) This step lists Agav's built-in tools. Choose only the tools this agent needs: - Press / to navigate the list - Press to toggle a tool on or off The selected names are written to the agent's manifest allowlist. If you leave every tool unchecked, the agent still has access to its own local tools and selected MCP servers, but not Agav's built-in tools. Step 6: Select MCP servers (optional) This step shows a list of MCP servers defined in your workspace . Each server appears with a checkbox. - Press / to navigate the list - Press to toggle a server on or off Selected servers are bundled into the agent's manifest, making them available whenever the agent runs. This is useful for agents that need access to specific tools — for example, a agent might use a GitHub MCP server for repository operations. If you don't need any MCP servers, or none are configured in your workspace, press to skip this step and continue. Step 7: Review and save The final step shows a summary of everything you've configured: - Name — - Description — "Helps with GitHub repository management tasks" - Destination path — where will be written - System prompt preview — the generated prompt text - Native tools — the built-in Agav tools you selected - MCP servers — any servers you selected - Tags — auto-generated from your name and description Review the summary. If anything looks wrong, press to go back and make changes. Press to create the agent. Agav: 1. Writes the manifest to disk 2. Registers the agent in the agent registry 3. Validates the manifest 4. Reloads the agent list You'll see a confirmation message once the agent is ready. It appears immediately in both the List and Create tabs. Editing an existing agent To modify a user-created agent, open the Create tab, navigate to it in the list, and press . The wizard opens with all fields pre-populated from the existing manifest. During edits: - Name is read-only — you cannot rename an agent after creation - Description can be updated freely - System prompt can be regenerated with or accepted as-is - Native tools can be added or removed - MCP servers can be added or removed The same five-step flow applies. Press on the final review step to save your changes. Working with templates Templates preserve deleted agents so you can restore them later. How templates are created — when you delete a globally installed, user-created agent (from either the List or Create tab), Agav automatically saves it as a template. Project-scoped user-created agents are deleted without a template. Nothing extra is required. Finding templates — templates appear in the Create tab alongside your active agents, marked with a label. Restoring a template — navigate to a template and press . The wizard opens with all fields pre-populated (name, description, system prompt, and MCP servers). Walk through the steps and press on the review step to recreate the agent. Deleting a template permanently — navigate to a template and press . This removes it from the template store with no way to recover it. Storage — templates are stored in ( on Windows). This file is managed automatically; you don't need to edit it by hand. Keyboard reference | Key | Action | |-----|--------| | / | Navigate list or switch wizard fields | | | Switch between name and description fields | | | Select / advance / save | | | Toggle MCP server selection (step 5) | | | Regenerate system prompt (step 4) | | / | Go back one step or exit wizard | | | Delete agent or template from list | Related - Agents — how agents work - Build a Native Agent — manual agent creation with custom tools - Agent Manifest — format reference - Install and Configure an Agent — marketplace agents

title: Build a Native Agent
content: Build a Native Agent A native agent combines an manifest with tools. This example builds a self-contained tool that needs no network access, dependencies, or credentials. The setup commands work from macOS, Linux, and Windows terminals. 1. Create the manifest Create : The manifest’s entry lets Agav discover the schema without importing your code. The label describes the tool but does not exempt it from confirmation in mode. Use for tools that change state. See the Agent Manifest reference for credential fields, schema sidecars, and built-in tool access. 2. Write the tool Create : Use for ES module syntax on every platform. The filename matches the manifest name . Return and reserve stdout for Agav’s tool result protocol. 3. Install and test Run from the directory containing : Add to install only for the current project, or to install under another name. CLI installation registers the agent as enabled. Start or restart Agav and ask: “Use to greet Ada.” In mode, review the agent and tool calls before approving them. For an agent that needs credentials, open . Platform limits: Installed JavaScript tools use separate Seatbelt or Bubblewrap profiles when available on macOS or Linux. Both profiles block network access, so an agent-local tool that calls an external API with will not work there. The Windows restricted-token shell sandbox does not cover native-agent JavaScript. See Agent sandbox before installing or distributing code. Using the LLM to implement tools In the List tab, inspect a global agent with , then press when Implement tools appears. To make a stub eligible, put in its exposed schema description and in the tool source. A configured provider is required. Review the generated implementation before running it. Sharing via the marketplace Add the agent directory and an entry to the Agav marketplace repository. Include the list for HTTP installation. See Agent Marketplace. A2A Agents — Experimental An A2A agent runs a separate executable and communicates over loopback HTTP. This integration is experimental and is not the same as the remote MCP transport. Manifest Use the interpreter executable available on your machine (for example, on Windows). Agav runs the command directly from the installed agent directory, not through a shell. Shell pipelines, variable expansion, and Windows wrappers are not supported. The subprocess inherits Agav’s launch environment and is not covered by the shell sandbox. Review the executable and its arguments before invoking it. Protocol | Endpoint | Method | Behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | | GET | Return a successful HTTP response when ready. | | | POST | Accept and return as JSON. | Use a loopback endpoint; remote hosts are unsupported. Agav polls health with a ten-second startup budget, then sends tasks to . Normal agent invocation does not use the experimental client. Per-agent credential injection, per-agent MCP servers, and confirmations for individual actions inside the A2A process are not supported. title: Author and Evolve a Skill
content: Author and Evolve a Skill Use a skill when you repeat the same procedure across several tasks. Scenario: review modules consistently Create in the hello-agav repository: Restart Agav, then run the skill manually: keeps the workflow predictable: it runs only when you call it. The tool allowlist also keeps the review read-only. Improve it from real use Inspect its configuration and usage: After several runs, change one instruction when you see a repeated problem — for example, add an edge-case check for malformed JSON if reviews keep missing it. Keep project skills in source control and review instruction changes like code. Expected result Every module review follows the same checks and produces the same compact report format. content: Install and Configure an Agent This guide walks through installing the Jira agent from the marketplace, configuring its credentials, and using it in a session. Use the same flow for other marketplace agents, but check their required credentials, tools, and permissions before installing. Prerequisites - Agav installed and connected to an LLM provider - Credentials for the service you're connecting (e.g. a Jira API token) - A trusted agent source. The Windows shell sandbox does not cover marketplace agent JavaScript; on macOS/Linux, Agav's separate agent sandbox can block outbound network access. Read the agent sandbox notes before using a network-dependent agent. Step 1: Open the marketplace Start Agav and type: Press to switch to the Marketplace tab. Agav fetches the catalog. You'll see agents listed three per page with name, description, tool count, and category. Step 2: Find and inspect the agent Use / to navigate and / to page through results. Press to search by name or keyword. Navigate to jira and press to inspect it. The inspect view shows the full description, tool list (with and labels), and required credentials. Press or to go back. Step 3: Install With the agent selected, press . A destination prompt appears: Press to install globally. Agav copies the agent files and registers it. You'll see once complete. On Windows, the global location resolves to . Step 4: Switch to the List tab Installation returns you to the List tab. If you switched away, press to return. Find the entry with origin . New installs are enabled by default, but the agent still needs its required credentials. Step 5: Inspect the agent Highlight the entry and press for Agent diagnostics. The diagnostics view shows: - Required Config — credentials the agent needs - Tools — individual tool names with / labels - Model / Effort — (can be overridden) Step 6: Open the config editor Press from diagnostics, or from the List tab, to open the credential and settings editor. Each required credential appears in the list with its status: Navigate with / and press on a field to edit it. Step 7: Enter credentials For JIRAURL: type or paste your Jira base URL (e.g. ), then press . For JIRAEMAIL: enter your Atlassian account email, then . For JIRAAPITOKEN: paste your Atlassian API token using your terminal's paste shortcut, then press . The editor saves each value in the agent's own encrypted (for this install, , or in PowerShell). Do not commit the credential file if you install into a project. Press to return to the inspect view. Step 8: Check readiness In diagnostics, check that all required values are configured. If the agent was disabled, return to the List tab with , highlight , and press to enable it. opens details; it does not toggle the agent. Step 9: Use the agent Return to your main chat and ask Agav something Jira-related: If Agav does not delegate, ask it to use the Jira agent explicitly. In mode, agent tools can require approval even when the catalog marks them . In mode, third-party tools are blocked. Review any request before approving it. A ready status only means the required settings are present; it does not validate your service credentials or prove the tool can reach Jira. If the indicator persists, press again and verify the values, particularly that there are no leading or trailing spaces. Agent not appearing in the list — press in the List tab to reload installed agents. If Jira is missing from the marketplace, press there and check which marketplace catalog is configured. title: Operate a Long-Running Task
content: Operate a Long-Running Task Long tasks stay manageable when discovery, implementation, and review have explicit boundaries. Scenario: add a greeting history feature to hello-agav Give Agav the outcome, source of truth, constraints, and checkpoints. This keeps the research, repository edits, tests, and documentation in one auditable workflow: The first phase deliberately requires reading the existing code before implementation: this makes the new feature consistent with the established patterns in the project. Add a task-specific skill For a task that will recur, add a project skill before starting. Its clear description lets Agav automatically select it when a prompt mentions greeting history or logging; you can also invoke it explicitly. Create : Restart Agav after creating the skill. Use the same task through the explicit skill command when you want to guarantee the procedure is applied: Add a deterministic check plugin Use a local plugin for a mechanical check rather than relying on the model to visually compare output. Create ( on Windows): Restart Agav and verify that lists . After implementing the history feature, prompt Agav: Check progress with . If a requirement changes, steer future work without discarding completed investigation: Use subagents only for independent work — for example, one can review the history module while another updates the README. Keep the main agent responsible for the shared integration, edits, tests, and final diff. Before implementation, review the proposed design. Before completion, review changed paths, test output, and unresolved assumptions. Use if the conversation becomes long; save memory only for a durable decision that should affect later sessions. Keep the token out of project configuration and version control. In the terminal that will start Agav, set the token and restrict the server to repository and issue tools: macOS / Linux: Windows PowerShell: The read-only switch prevents the GitHub MCP server from exposing write tools, even when its enabled toolsets include them. The entries pass the exported values into Docker; they do not put the token in the configuration file. Agav merges the global configuration first and then the project configuration, field by field. title: Coordinate Parallel Subagents
content: Coordinate Parallel Subagents Use subagents when independent investigations need more context than a few tool calls. Scenario: audit every module in hello-agav The project has separate modules for CLI parsing, greeting logic, and counter persistence. They can be reviewed independently, then compared for consistency. Each assignment includes its files, checks, output, and no-edit constraint because subagents work independently and cannot ask follow-up questions. Review the combined result Use / to select a subagent and to inspect it. Press in the detail view to cancel the focused subagent, or to return to the overview without cancelling. Sensitive confirmations still appear in the main terminal. While a confirmation is visible, denies that tool call rather than cancelling the focused subagent. When all workers finish, ask the main agent to resolve disagreements and remove duplicate findings. Delegate edits only when workers own different files; worktrees reduce interference but do not make overlapping changes safe. Cancellation and time limits From the overview, Esc cancels the parent turn and signals all its subagents to stop. Cancelling from a subagent detail view targets only that worker; its pending confirmations are rejected so it can leave the approval wait. Ctrl+C with no Agav selection exits the application rather than cancelling just one worker. Cancellation can arrive during worktree setup, before the worker starts its agent loop. A cancelled worker does not intentionally merge its partial worktree edits back into the parent. If cancellation arrives during worktree integration, Agav rolls the merge back before discarding the worker. A rollback failure retains the worker and reports an error for recovery. Edits made without a worktree, external actions already performed, and delivery that finished before cancellation are not undone. Review the resulting diff. There is no separate wall-clock timeout for the entire subagent task. Workers inherit the configured iteration limit, and individual tools have their own timeouts. Shell and test subprocesses receive the worker's cancellation signal; custom tools still need to honor it. Cancelling an MCP tool stops Agav's wait, not necessarily the server-side work, and cancelling a Docker command does not guarantee container cleanup. Expected result You receive three bounded audits and one reconciled list of risks across main.py, greeting.py, and counter.py, while the main conversation retains final ownership. Next: Run Tools in Parallel.

title: Run Tools in Parallel
content: Run Tools in Parallel Use parallel tools for short, independent checks that belong in the same conversation. Scenario: understand hello-agav before adding a feature Before adding a new feature, you need to understand three separate parts of the project: - how the CLI parses arguments and calls modules - how the greeting is built - how the run counter works Ask Agav to inspect them together: Agav can run independent reads and searches concurrently, then return the evidence to the same conversation. Keep dependencies in order Do not parallelize steps when one changes what the next step reads. State the order explicitly: Keep overlapping edits and state-changing commands sequential. A successful or invalidates earlier verification. Tests or shell checks in the same parallel tool batch as that edit do not count as post-edit verification, even if their result arrives last. Wait for the edit batch to finish, then run checks in a later batch. Independent checks against the same finished revision can run together. If any check in that batch fails, a passing sibling does not cancel the failure; fix the cause and verify again in a later batch. A result with no recognized passing tests is inconclusive, not proof that the change passed. Passing tests still do not replace any required build, manual run, warning review, or expected-output comparison. See structured test runs for the exact behavior. Tool results remain bounded per result when run concurrently. Parallel reads can still add substantial aggregate context, and large simultaneous captures share the process's temporary-output retention budget. Prefer a focused depth, targeted searches, and file ranges; follow truncation notices when more evidence is needed. Use parallel subagents when each investigation is large enough to need its own context. Expected result You get one concise map of the CLI arguments, greeting format, and counter persistence without waiting for each independent read in sequence. Next: Coordinate Parallel Subagents.

content: CLI Reference Modes --max-turns caps agent iterations per prompt across interactive, print (), and run () modes. - Interactive: the cap applies to each user turn in the session. The budget resets for every new prompt and is shared with subagents, named agents, and skills. Tool execution itself does not spend an additional turn. - Print and run modes: the cap applies across model requests for the one-shot task, including retries. The value must contain decimal digits only and be between 1 and 9007199254740991; signs, fractions, scientific notation, and hexadecimal notation are rejected. Both and are accepted. The flag overrides in configuration for the current session only. On resume, the session history is kept but the cap is reapplied to new prompts. --config, -c (long form ) overrides a single configuration value for the current session, layered on top of the config files and environment — tweak one setting for one run without editing . - Repeatable; when the same key is given twice, the later one wins. - Dotted paths set one nested value without touching its siblings: . The control plane acts as the SAML Service Provider: Agav opens a browser to the control plane, which runs the SAML dance with the IdP server-side and mints the same identity proof the other flows produce. Audit events (SIEM) When an audit sink is configured, enterprise enrollment and sign-out emit a secret-free JSON event per action (, , , ) to the sink via . Each event carries the action, the login flow, the control-plane origin, the subject (on success), a reason code (on failure), an ISO-8601 timestamp, and — never an , gateway token, authorization code, or PKCE verifier. The failure is a fixed, allowlisted code (e.g. , , , , , ), never a raw error message — so a message that happens to echo server content can never leak to the SIEM. Full error details still go to local stderr. Emission is best-effort: a slow, unreachable, or misconfigured sink never blocks or fails login. Configure the sink (an HTTPS endpoint) by either: - the field in the organization policy (admin-shipped; preferred), or - the environment variable (local/dev). With no sink configured, no events are emitted.

content: Configuration Agav merges defaults, , and in that order. Environment variables then override provider credentials and Ollama address settings, session overrides layer on top of the result, dedicated CLI flags win over those, and organization-managed policy wins over everything (see Precedence). Precedence For most settings the effective value is the last one found in this chain: 1. built-in defaults 2. global config — 3. project config — 4. environment variables (credentials and Ollama address settings only) 5. session overrides — (repeatable; see the CLI reference) 6. dedicated CLI flags (applied at startup) 7. organization-managed config (see Organization-managed configuration) — applied last and not overridable by the user When an administrator ships an organization policy, its enforced fields win over every source above, including environment variables and CLI flags. A user can make a setting stricter (for example choosing a more restrictive ) but cannot loosen or bypass an org-enforced value. Provider credentials and endpoint overrides are resolved separately and follow a stricter chain, because the sensitive fields listed under Project config restrictions are stripped from project config before merging. For each API key the effective value is the first one found in: 1. the provider's environment variable (e.g. ) 2. global config 3. built-in default (normally empty) Because the key fields are removed from project config, a value like placed in is silently ignored — it never reaches the provider. Project config restrictions To prevent a malicious repository from redirecting API requests or escalating permissions, the following fields are ignored in project configuration and can only be set in global configuration (), via environment variables, or from your own command line with (explicit user intent, session-only): - Endpoint overrides: , , , , - API keys: , , , , , , - Permission escalation: - Sandbox policy: , , - Automation opt-in and unattended scheduling: , - Enterprise routing: , (use the organization policy or their documented CLI/environment options, not user config) These fields are stripped from before it is merged, so a value placed there is silently ignored rather than applied — Agav does not warn about it. This ensures that cloning an untrusted repository cannot silently redirect your credentials to a third-party server or bypass tool confirmations. Use the supported global, environment, or CLI setting for each field. > This is not the same as gitignore. Ignoring in a repository only stops you from accidentally committing your own project config. It does not protect you when you clone someone else's repo: a malicious author can commit a poisoned anyway (for example with , which overrides ), and it arrives on your disk as a tracked file the moment you clone. Your local never applies to it. The deny-list above is the actual defense against that clone-and-run threat, because it strips the dangerous fields at load time regardless of how the file got there. Do not rely on gitignore for credential safety. Organization-managed configuration Organizations can enforce a policy that takes precedence over every other configuration source and that users cannot loosen. This is the mechanism IT or a platform team uses to pin a gateway, restrict which providers and models developers may use, and set a minimum permission level across a fleet. Where the policy comes from Agav looks for an administrator-provided policy file in this order: 1. the path named by the environment variable 2. a known system path: - macOS: , then - Linux: - Windows: Deliver the file through your device-management (MDM) tooling or your fleet provisioning. If there is no file or cached policy, no organization policy is enforced. If no policy file exists, Agav falls back to policy cached by enterprise enrollment. A present but unreadable or invalid file is a policy error, not a reason to fall back. What a policy can enforce | Field | Effect | | --- | --- | | , | Hard pin — the org value is used regardless of user config. | | , | Hard pin — route all OpenAI-compatible traffic through the organization's gateway. | | | Floor — the user may choose a stricter mode but never a looser one (strictness order: > > ). | | | Allowlist — selecting a provider outside the list is rejected at startup. Omit the list for no restriction; an explicit empty list is rejected. | | | Allowlist — selecting a model outside the list is rejected at startup. Omit the list for no restriction; an explicit empty list is rejected. | | | Additive — the org's required tools are merged with the user's allowlist. | | | Address of a self-hosted control plane used by enterprise enrollment. Optional — omit it to use Agav's hosted control plane. | | | HTTPS endpoint that receives secret-free / audit events for your SIEM. Optional. The same policy shape can be delivered by authenticated enterprise enrollment instead of a file; the enforcement behavior is identical regardless of source.
