title: job-recovery
content: Recovering capacity from uncertain background jobs An or job has no verified workload outcome. It normally continues to occupy shared background-job capacity (default four jobs), including capacity needed by workflow runners. Age, empty logs, missing IPC or an empty startup nonce do not prove that nothing executed or that descendants stopped. Abandonment releases accounting capacity; it does not stop processes or establish success, failure, or safe retry. It is an explicit operator decision, not automatic recovery. Prerequisites - Use an updated Agav build that lists in . Use the same OS user/profile that owns the job store (normally ). - Enable in the profile's . refuses abandonment; do not bypass your organization's permission policy. - Review the saved command, working directory, logs, uncertainty reason and external side effects. Identify any linked workflow runner or child job. Keep evidence and an incident record before acting. - Coordinate with other operators. Updated supervisors honor the startup and publication fence. Already-running old supervisors do not gain that protection when you upgrade the CLI. Do not infer termination or kill historical PIDs from this operation. Inspect, then explicitly abandon In an Agav session: The jobs manager also shows details and both log streams. Polling can reconnect or update reconciliation state; it is not a strictly read-only forensic operation. If the supervisor reconnects, prefer observing its actual result or the supported stop path. Only after accepting that outcome and descendants remain unverified, choose one of: Replace with the entire stored ID, not the short list prefix. The acknowledgement flag is mandatory for CLI and slash commands. Success reports capacity released and explicitly warns that no processes were stopped and no retry was authorized. Interactive jobs manager 1. Open , select the or job, and press Enter/i to inspect details and logs. Review external side effects too. 2. Press a: Abandon from the list or detail view. Read the acknowledgement: outcome and descendants remain unverified; no processes will be stopped and no retry is authorized. 3. Press y to acknowledge, or n/Esc to cancel without writing. This confirmation is required even in mode. still refuses the operation. After successful abandonment, the job disappears from the manager's default active list. Jobs abandoned previously through CLI/slash commands are hidden there too. Press h: Show abandoned to include retained records, labelled [abandoned]; press h again to hide them. They remain inspectable, but Stop, Abandon and Delete are not offered for them. still includes all stored records and still shows their audit. This is a reversible display filter derived from the abandonment tombstone, not permanent archival or deletion. The default active list also includes ordinary terminal history: it is not a count of running processes. An empty list never proves that nothing is running. A fresh reconnect, state change or failed audit write is reported as a refusal/failure, not successful abandonment; the job is not hidden without a durable audit. What changes and what stays - An atomic audit tombstone records the abandonment time, acknowledgement, previous uncertain state and nonce. The job keeps its uncertain lifecycle and existing evidence; abandonment does not synthesize an exit code, end time or completion event. - Only that job's capacity slot is released. Other uncertain jobs still count. Existing work may still consume real resources, so accounting capacity is not a resource-safety guarantee. - The tombstone survives restart and is immutable through the updated repository. Repeating the acknowledged operation returns the same audit. The original request ID still returns the original job: it is never redispatched. - Specs, logs and references are retained. Cleanup and deletion are not recovery shortcuts; an abandoned uncertain job is not eligible for terminal-only deletion. Do not rewrite JSON, remove locks or wipe the profile. - Updated supervisors check the fence before workload spawn and serialize completion publication with abandonment under the job lock. A late completion after abandonment does not publish a new completion event. This does not stop an already-spawned workload. Refusals and failures A fresh reconnect, changed record (including nonce), known terminal outcome, or held job/coordinator lock prevents abandonment. Inspect again; do not force past evidence or lock checks. Storage publication failure is not success and does not release capacity without the durable audit. Resolve the reported storage/permission issue, inspect the record, and retry the same explicit operation if still appropriate. Workflow limitations Abandonment does not resume a workflow, replace an uncertain runner, retry a child job, or authorize replay of a mutating tool. Runner and child job IDs are distinct; abandoning one does not resolve the other. A queued workflow that never admitted a runner may be able to use ordinary resume after capacity is available, subject to its normal consent and limits. A workflow linked to an uncertain runner or child still needs separate inspection; no automatic force/retry is provided by abandonment. See Workflows. On Windows the fallback has no Job Object helper and reports unverified ownership. Lost IPC or direct-child termination cannot prove descendant termination. This operation does not remove that limitation.

title: Keybindings
content: Keybindings Agav loads defaults, then , then . Project bindings replace global or default bindings for the same action. On Windows, resolves to . | Action | Default | | --- | --- | | Cancel current turn / focused subagent, or dismiss active UI | | | Expand tool detail | | | Plan detail panel | | | Toggle thinking text | | | Toggle compaction summary | | | Pause / resume generation | , or | | Scroll up / down | / , or / | | Scroll to top / bottom | / | | Select subagent | / | | Inspect subagent | | | Back to overview | | | Insert newline | , or / when the terminal sends them | | Submit | | | Prompt history | / | | Exit, or copy an active Agav selection | | | Clear input | | | Delete previous word | | | Edit last prompt | | | Retry last turn | | | Command palette | | | Show keybindings | | | Clear screen | | | Detach a worker-owned session, including at approval prompts () | | | Cut prompt text | | | Open the request queue when requests are queued; otherwise exit while idle with an empty prompt | | Mouse controls Interactive Agav sessions support terminal mouse input when the terminal forwards mouse reports. Keyboard shortcuts remain available everywhere, including terminals without mouse support. - Left-click selectable rows, tabs, links, prompt suggestions, footer actions, and confirmation controls where the current screen exposes them. Clicking a row in opens that session. Destructive actions still require their own visible control or keyboard shortcut. - Hover over supported list rows to move the same highlight used by the arrow keys, without opening or applying anything. - Mouse-wheel navigation moves the active selection in pickers and lists, including login options, permission modes, customization, agents, marketplace results, workflow environment checklists, and resource managers. Screens with their own scrollable details handle the wheel locally. - Drag over Agav output selects text and copies it when the drag ends. Dragging across an input prompt positions or selects text according to the prompt editor. A drag or wheel movement over a confirmation control does not count as a click. - In the model picker, Ctrl+Y copies the highlighted model ID without switching models. Click a model or press Enter to switch. - In a shell-tool approval, click the command preview to expand or collapse it without making an approval decision. In resource-manager forms, use Tab and Shift+Tab to move forward and backward. - Right- and middle-click are left to the terminal's normal behavior; Agav does not use them for in-app actions. A terminal context menu may temporarily interrupt mouse reporting, and Agav re-establishes tracking for later left-clicks. Mouse controls are intentionally conservative around confirmations: the press and release must remain on the same visible left-click control, and a newly displayed prompt cannot be answered by the tail of an earlier double-click. If mouse input is unavailable, use the displayed keyboard labels. For worker-owned turns, Ctrl+D closes the UI without cancelling or answering pending consent. Enable in global config before starting the task. The shortcut works as soon as the worker is ready. With enabled, randomized status-bar tips can show a detach hint using your configured chord; the shortcut does not depend on the hint being visible. Return with or . Ctrl+X cuts prompt text; Ctrl+Q manages the queue/idle exit. Neither is detach. See Detached sessions for requirements and cancellation semantics. Cancel versus exit Press Esc to cancel the active turn and stay in Agav. For a worker-owned turn, this writes a durable, generation-bound cancellation request; it does not synchronously kill the worker or undo side effects. See Detached sessions. In an actual detail view it cancels only that worker; from the overview it cancels the whole turn. Skill and named-agent progress entries share that UI but have no individual focused-cancel handler: return to the overview with Tab before cancelling their parent turn. Manual-only slash-command skills receive no turn cancellation signal. An open picker or preview handles Esc locally. At a tool confirmation, Esc means No for that tool call, not cancel the whole turn. Press Ctrl+C with no text selected in Agav to exit, whether idle or busy. Like , this requests cancellation of a selected live worker, unlike or the detach chord. Switching sessions or unmounting the presentation does not cancel it. If an Agav output selection is active, Ctrl+C copies it and keeps Agav open; clear the selection before pressing Ctrl+C to exit. Cmd+C on macOS and Ctrl+Shift+C where supported are copy shortcuts, not exit shortcuts. Terminal-native copy behavior takes precedence when your terminal intercepts a shortcut. The action is configurable. Ctrl+C is also handled by the terminal UI before configurable actions, so rebinding does not turn Ctrl+C into a stay-in-session cancel shortcut. Use Esc for that. Voice recording controls During , the prompt remains editable while listening and finalizing. Enter sends the displayed draft once microphone cleanup is acknowledged; click Stop to finish without sending and continue editing. Esc or Ctrl+C cancels dictation or a pending voice send instead of exiting Agav. During model-download consent, Y approves and N/Esc declines; Enter alone does not approve. These voice controls use their fixed keys rather than the configurable prompt-submit/cancel bindings. See Voice Input. Override bindings Values can be a string or an array. Chords separate strokes with spaces: Names are case-insensitive. , , and normalize to , , and . Pause and intervene mid-turn For foreground in-process turns, while the agent is streaming or running tools, press Ctrl+B (or Alt+P) to pause generation, and press it again to resume. Pausing does not cancel the turn — it holds the loop so you can read what has happened so far. While paused you can also redirect the task: type a message and press Enter. Agav cancels the paused request, waits for its pending state to clear, and starts a new request with your direction in the same conversation. This is distinct from Esc, which cancels the current turn while keeping Agav open, and Ctrl+C, which exits when no Agav text selection is active. Worker-owned turns do not support pause, including after resume. Use to redirect an attached worker at its next safe step instead; see Planning and Steering. The default binding is ; override it like any other action, for example: Terminal protocols determine which key combinations Agav can distinguish. Many terminals encode as Enter and do not distinguish ; use / () when your terminal supports it. Multi-line input Press Shift+Enter to insert a newline instead of sending the message. This requires the Kitty keyboard protocol — without it your terminal transmits the exact same byte for Shift+Enter and Enter, so the modifier is lost before Agav sees it. Kitty, Ghostty, WezTerm, foot, Alacritty, and recent iTerm2 support it; terminals that don't are left untouched. Ctrl+J is the default fallback on macOS, Linux, and Windows when Shift+Enter does nothing. Terminal shortcuts can still intercept keys before Agav receives them. Alt+Enter ( on macOS) also works where the terminal sends Option as Meta. The prompt footer accounts for whether enhanced keyboard encoding is active. Set to force legacy encoding if a terminal answers the protocol query but handles it badly, or to force the protocol on. > macOS Terminal.app implements neither the Kitty protocol nor CSI-u. Use , or enable Option+Enter via Settings → Profiles → Keyboard → check "Use Option as Meta key". Copying output Drag across Agav output to select text; releasing the drag copies it. While an Agav selection remains active, Ctrl+C copies it without exiting, even during a running turn. Cmd+C on macOS and Ctrl+Shift+C also copy an active selection when the terminal sends those keys to Agav. Your terminal may instead manage its own selection and intercept copy shortcuts. Use Cmd+C on macOS or Ctrl+Shift+C on Linux and Windows Terminal for terminal-native copy, as supported by your terminal. In legacy encodings Ctrl+Shift+C may arrive as Ctrl+C; without an Agav selection, that exits. To save the retained conversation to a file, use for Markdown or for structured data. Add for best-effort credential and home-path redaction; review the file before sharing. Earlier trimmed or compacted content cannot be recovered. See Sessions and Memory.

title: Security
content: Security Agav can read files, edit code, and execute commands. Choose controls appropriate to the repository and environment. Permission modes | Mode | Behavior | | --- | --- | | | Confirm sensitive actions and show edit diffs | | | Skip normal confirmations for faster trusted workflows | | | Block writes and mutation-oriented operations | Set a default in configuration or use and at startup. can auto-approve named tools or scoped command patterns. Changing the mode during a session In an interactive session you can switch the permission mode at any time with [](/reference/slash-commands). Run bare to open a picker, or pass a mode directly (). In the picker, use the mouse wheel or arrow keys to move, and left-click a mode to preview it; click Enter Apply or use Enter to save. The chosen mode is saved with the session and restored when you resume it, so a session you escalated to or tightened to comes back in that mode. It does not change the launch default used for or for future sessions — set in configuration for that. Explicit () and flags at startup take precedence over a session's saved mode. An organization floor is always applied last: and the picker let you choose a stricter mode but clamp any attempt to loosen below the floor, and report the mode actually in force. Changing the mode is only available in an interactive session — in headless and print mode, from configuration is authoritative. > (the interactive session mode) is distinct from the CLI flag, which supplies a JSON tool policy for . See CLI reference. Project config safety Sensitive configuration fields are blocked from project-level to prevent credential exfiltration and permission escalation when working in untrusted repositories. See Configuration → Project config restrictions for the full list. deny-writes mode In mode, , , and , and tools classified as destructive, are blocked even when allowlisted. Extension tools that still require confirmation are also blocked; an external tool’s claim to be read-only does not exempt it. A not classified as destructive can execute when allowlisted. mutations (POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE) are also blocked. This is not a universal read-only boundary: command classification is heuristic, and even a remote GET can have server-side effects. Do not rely on this mode alone to prevent external side effects. Safe tools These tools are treated as safe by the permission gate and normally do not require confirmation. This designation does not mean they have no side effects ( and write Agav state): , , , , , , , (GET/HEAD only), , , , mutations require explicit approval for each call, even under or an entry. Blanket “always” approval does not authorize them; without a confirmation handler they are refused. See HTTP request safety. External tool trust External agents and MCP tools cannot mark themselves as non-destructive to skip confirmation. Only built-in safe tools are trusted with the flag. In mode, untrusted extension tools need confirmation unless an applicable policy already allows them. A tool’s own declaration does not grant that approval. Shell sandbox Agav auto-detects the best available OS-level sandbox at startup: | Platform | Backend | Mechanism | | --- | --- | --- | | macOS | Seatbelt | with deny-default writes and explicit allowances | | Linux | Bubblewrap | with read-only root, a private workspace snapshot, and credential masking | | Docker | Container | , memory and CPU limits | | Windows | Restricted token | Enabled by default: native helper, workspace ACL grants, Job Object | If no backend is available, and are refused when is enabled; otherwise automatic execution is unsandboxed. and both default to on Windows and elsewhere. Set before starting Agav to intentionally disable sandbox detection and permit overrides of . Without that user opt-out, model-requested overrides are rejected, including through skills and subagents. Tool approval, “always”, and auto-accept do not authorize sandbox bypass. Invalid backend values are rejected, and failure to launch a selected sandbox does not retry the command unsandboxed. The footer shows the shell default, not proof of isolation for every tool or command. reports the execution backend when it differs from that default. Direct user shell commands intentionally remain unsandboxed with an inherited environment; this does not grant the model the same privilege. These shell policies do not provide OS isolation for native file tools. The Seatbelt and Bubblewrap sections below describe and execution. Agent tool processes use separate profiles: their Seatbelt profile is deny-default, blocks network, and allows writes only in the working directory and temp; their Bubblewrap runner uses , binds host , and masks existing credential and directories. Do not assume shell and agent-tool network policies are identical. Bundled agents are trusted and run unsandboxed; global and project agent tools use Seatbelt or Bubblewrap when detected. Windows restricted-token and Docker shell backends do not sandbox agent-local JavaScript. If neither supported agent backend is available, agent tools run in an unsandboxed subprocess; does not cover them. Seatbelt (macOS) The Seatbelt profile denies all filesystem writes by default, then restores explicit allowances. Other operations remain broadly allowed subject to the restrictions below; it is not a deny-all capability boundary: - Reads — allowed across the filesystem, except , , and - Writes — allowed only in the working directory, temporary directories, , selected Git state paths, and tooling directories (, , , , ). Credential directories remain denied. - Protected configuration — Git config, hooks, and worktree pointers, workspace , , , and shell startup paths are protected, including names that do not exist yet. Ordinary Git state remains writable. - Network — allowed by default. With an explicit deny policy (see Network policy), direct off-host networking is blocked; host-local TCP/IP and Unix sockets remain trusted channels, so local relays can still forward traffic - Process execution — allowed, except - IPC — Mach lookup, sysctl reads, and POSIX shared memory are allowed for basic process operation Bubblewrap (Linux) - Filesystem — root is mounted read-only (); commands write to a private workspace snapshot, not the live checkout. Changes are validated and published only after a successful, uncancelled command. Publication rejects changes to the protected configuration paths listed above, including previously absent paths. - Tooling — , , , , and use throwaway scratch mounts. Installed tools under and remain visible read-only; is restored read-only over the Cargo scratch mount. - Credentials — , , and are replaced with empty tmpfs mounts, hiding their contents - Network — allowed by default. With an explicit deny policy (see Network policy), Agav passes : loopback reaches only services started within the same command, not host services or other commands - Lifecycle — a private PID namespace () and prevent background descendants from surviving the invocation. Docker - Network — disabled () - Resources — 512 MB memory, 1 CPU - Filesystem — only the working directory is mounted into the container (at ) - User — the container runs as your host UID/GID () so files written to the working directory stay owned by you. Agav detects the daemon's security mode: under rootless Docker (which already maps you to the host user via user namespaces) the explicit UID mapping is omitted, and under daemon-level userns-remap it adds so the mapping resolves to the real host user rather than a subordinate UID. Windows Restricted-token sandbox On Windows, and both default to , so and use Agav's native restricted-token helper. A missing helper blocks these executions, not Agav startup. Project config cannot change either setting. can also request the backend override when the helper is present. - Writes — commands run under a write-restricted Windows token. A write succeeds only where Agav granted its sandbox identity access: the working directory and a dedicated sandbox temp directory. , , and the npm, pip, and Yarn caches point at that temp directory. Writes elsewhere in your profile and on the system are denied. - Protected configuration — inside the workspace, Git hooks and configuration, , , , and shell startup files (, , , , , ) are denied. Ordinary Git operations still work. - Lifecycle — commands run in a Job Object, so descendants are terminated when the command exits, times out, or is cancelled. Detached background servers do not survive the command. - Permission changes — the grants and denials are entries Agav adds to the permissions of your workspace and the sandbox temp directory. The first command in a large workspace can take longer while Windows applies them. Agav records every location it changes; run to remove its entries. Limits: - Reads and networking are not confined. Commands are refused, not run, while is ; use with the Docker override when you need network isolation ( has no Docker override). - Locations that already grant write access to stay writable. - Protected paths that don't exist yet can't carry a denial, so a command could create one of them. - In linked Git worktrees whose metadata lives outside the workspace, Git commands that write metadata fail. If the helper is unavailable or can't start, the command fails; it never falls back to running unsandboxed. Background jobs With , the tool starts commands that run outside the shell sandbox, with no timeout and full access as your OS user. Each start, schedule create, stop, and schedule revoke is a separate approved action. The prompt shows the full command, directory, and isolation, and an approval stays valid for that exact spec until it changes. blocks new jobs and schedules but still lets you confirm a stop or revoke. In print and mode these actions are refused without an existing grant. See Background jobs. Cancellation is not isolation Esc cancels an interactive turn while keeping Agav open; Ctrl+C exits unless it copies an active Agav selection. For worker-owned turns, ordinary cancellation and exit request durable, generation-bound cancellation, not synchronous termination. Only or the configured detach chord intentionally exits while leaving the worker running; session switches and presentation unmounts do not cancel. See Keybindings. Native and Seatbelt shell commands use process-group cleanup on failure, cancellation, timeout, and orderly exit; successful background children can survive ordinary completion. Cleanup is best-effort and cannot guarantee termination of descendants that detach from the owned group. Bubblewrap uses a private PID namespace, and the Windows sandbox uses a Job Object, so their background descendants do not survive an invocation. Cleanup cannot undo external actions. Agent subprocesses and Seatbelt/unsandboxed test runners receive cancellation signals without the shell runner's process-group cleanup guarantees. Bubblewrap and Windows sandboxed test runs retain their backend lifecycle isolation. Cancelling an MCP request stops the local wait, not necessarily server-side execution, and does not kill its shared server. Docker cancellation targets the local CLI, not guaranteed container/daemon cleanup. Check remote jobs, containers, and services separately after interruption. Tool-activated skills receive the parent turn signal, but focused skill entries have no individual cancel handler. Manual-only slash-command skills receive no turn signal. Skill shell blocks execute outside the restricted tool registry but use the default shell sandbox, filtered environment, process-group cleanup, and the skill's cancellation signal when supplied. uses its own 30-second timeout instead of the turn signal once a request starts. See Skills before trusting executable skill instructions. Temporary output privacy Large tool results may be saved outside the repository in private OS temporary files. They can contain secrets printed by commands or returned by APIs even when environment-variable filtering is enabled. Unix files use mode and directories , but the contents are not encrypted. Normal exit attempts cleanup; crash leftovers may remain until a later eligible stale-owner sweep. Do not put credentials in command output, and copy needed logs to an appropriately protected location before exiting. See output limits and retention for quotas and exact cleanup behavior. MCP command validation On Windows, MCP server subprocesses use for shim compatibility. Before spawning, Agav validates both the command and all arguments against a set of blocked shell metacharacters: ` $ ( ) { } [ ] ! % " \n \r `cmd.exeshell: falseKEYSECRETTOKENPASSWORDCREDENTIALAUTHsandboxRequired: true~/.agav/config.json--sandbox-requiredruncommandrunteststruefalseruncommandsandboxnoneAGAVNOSANDBOX=1sandbox: "docker"runtestssandboxRequiredruncommandruntests--sandbox-network deny--sandbox-no-network"sandboxNetwork": "deny"~/.agav/config.json--sandbox-network allow--sandbox-allow-networkdeny.agav/config.jsonsandboxNetworkdeny--network=nonefetchurlAuthorizationCookieProxy-Authorizationreadfilewritefileeditfile~/.agav//.git//.agav/~/.ssh/%USERPROFILE%\.ssh\~/.aws/%USERPROFILE%\.aws\~/.gnupg/%USERPROFILE%\.gnupg\~/.kube/config%USERPROFILE%\.kube\configauto-acceptrm -rf /rm -rf ~rm -rf .git reset --hardgit push --forcegit clean -fgit branch -Dsudo rmsudo dddd if=mkfs./dev/sdchmod -R 777chown -RdropdbDROP DATABASEkillallpkill -9curl ... | shwget ... | sh/bashtruncate --size 0gitRemove-Item -Recurse -Forcermdir /sdelFormat-VolumeStop-Processask~/.agav/config.jsonenc:keychain:~/.agav/.config.lock0600config.jsonVERTEXAICREDENTIALS_PATHvertexAICredentialsPathroles/aiplatform.user./.agav/config.json--max-turns` to limit unattended work.

title: Troubleshooting
content: Troubleshooting Agav is not found or runs an older version Run on macOS/Linux or in PowerShell to see which copy your shell resolves. Check in a fresh terminal. The installer normally puts the command in on macOS/Linux or in PowerShell. If that directory is missing from , add it or invoke the binary by its full path. If a different installation comes first, fix the order or remove the old copy. For in Windows PowerShell 5.1, use . For a Windows executable that needs the baseline build (for example, after an update on a machine without AVX2), rerun the PowerShell installer rather than . A release branch or its version badge is not proof that the binary has been published; check Releases. No provider credentials found Set the credential for your chosen provider in the same shell that launches Agav. For example, use on macOS/Linux or in PowerShell. Vertex AI needs pointing to a readable service-account JSON file; local Ollama needs a running server rather than a cloud key. If you pass , Agav will not fall back to another provider. Use the user config (, or in PowerShell), not a repository config, for saved keys. If your user config still contains a legacy reference, re-enter the key or set the matching environment variable. Do not include credentials in diagnostics you share. No Ollama models found Confirm the server is reachable and has a model: Use for remote or hosted installations. If the server requires authentication, set and pass explicitly; automatic model discovery does not send that key. For errors from llama.cpp or LM Studio instead, see local model troubleshooting. A file mention is rejected paths must stay inside the directory where Agav started. Start Agav higher in the repository, correct the relative path, or remove a symlink that resolves outside the workspace. A prompt can mention at most five unique files. A document preview is incomplete Use with a narrower line or page range. PDF and Office page requests return at most ten pages. Install LibreOffice or set when Office conversion is unavailable. A shortcut does not work Press the show-keybindings chord (default Ctrl+K, then Ctrl+S) and inspect global and project JSON overrides. Terminal encoding may collapse into Enter or hide ; use for a newline, or try on macOS / elsewhere if your terminal sends it. Interrupting a task exits Agav Use Esc to cancel the current turn and stay in Agav. Ctrl+C with no Agav text selection exits; with a selection, it copies instead. In an actual detail view, Esc targets that worker; skill and named-agent entries have no individual focused-cancel handler, so return to the overview before cancelling the parent; in a confirmation prompt, it denies that tool call. Close a picker or preview first if it consumes Esc. See Keybindings. For worker-owned turns, interrupting requests durable, generation-bound cancellation; it does not synchronously kill execution. Use or the configured detach shortcut (default Ctrl+D) to exit without requesting cancellation. See Detached sessions. Cancellation preserves already-applied edits and external side effects. Review before retrying. Retry backoff is cancellable, but custom tools must honor cancellation, MCP server work can continue, and Docker containers may need separate cleanup. See cancellation limits. Command output or file contents are truncated Tool text is capped at 40,000 UTF-8 bytes and 2,000 lines. A head/tail excerpt is not complete output. Follow the notice's saved log path with line ranges, or follow its continuation range in the original file. A single enormous line needs targeted extraction rather than repeating the same range. There is no option to raise the cap. Saved shell/HTTP logs hold at most 16 MiB. Shell execution continues after the log fills; HTTP capture cancels the remaining body, so a partial HTTP log may not contain the response's final lines. Logs are temporary and normal exit attempts to remove them. Copy anything needed before leaving Agav. If the notice reports storage or retention quota failure, omitted output may be unavailable. The tool's original status is preserved and it is not rerun automatically. Do not retry a side-effecting command or POST just to recover output; narrow a safe diagnostic query instead. See Built-in Tools for recovery and retention details. A shell command or test is refused Check for the detected sandbox. macOS uses Seatbelt when available; Linux can use Bubblewrap (), which must be installed and usable on the host. On Windows, shell and test tools require the native sandbox helper by default. If it is missing, try the standalone release instead of a source checkout. The restricted-token backend does not provide network isolation and refuses commands under . See Sandboxing for platform differences. uses on macOS/Linux and on native Windows, even if you started Agav in PowerShell. Use the command syntax for that runner; PowerShell scripts require starting PowerShell explicitly. uses a separate runner and does not work on native Windows. A command hangs or a background job remains Shell commands run without interactive stdin or a controlling terminal. Run password prompts, interactive Git/SSH commands, and terminal applications in your own shell. Command timeouts bound execution and inherited-pipe waits; cancellation attempts process-tree cleanup, but detached descendants and remote work may survive. Successful shell commands can leave background children under Seatbelt or the unsandboxed runner; Bubblewrap and the Windows sandbox terminate those descendants when the invocation ends. Jobs started through have a separate lifecycle. A successful shell leader does not prove its background job finished; inspect or stop the service explicitly. A repository map seems incomplete maps source files and symbols, not every file. It stops at 200 source files. Ask for a narrower path and explicit depth: is root files only, includes immediate subdirectories, and omitted depth is unrestricted. A cap notice means the map may be incomplete. See repository maps. Tests passed but Agav asks for more verification A passing recognized result counts after a successful edit only when it runs in a later tool batch. Zero-test, skipped-only, unrecognized, timed-out, or failed runs do not establish verification. An edit and tests in the same parallel batch are not post-edit evidence; later edits require new checks. Passing tests also do not replace a required build, manual check, or warning review. Ask Agav to run a focused check after the final edit; see verification status. A running skill seems idle or tokens have not updated Tool-activated skills appear in the worker overview; select one with ↑ / ↓, then Enter to inspect it. Manual-only skills open their details directly. The panel retains up to ten recent tool actions, not a complete transcript. Reasoning appears only when the provider emits it, and token usage updates only as usage events arrive; no event does not mean no billed usage. Reported partial usage remains after failure or interruption. Manual-only slash-command skills receive neither a turn cancellation signal nor an interactive approval handler: in mode sensitive operations are refused and shell blocks are skipped. The detail panel itself is not an approval prompt. See Skills. An MCP server is missing Check its command and arguments outside Agav, then inspect . MCP startup failures are non-fatal, and configuration changes require a restart. A scheduled task did not run A task needs Agav running when the cron expression matches. For unattended prompts, invoke or from an OS or CI scheduler. Recurring background job schedules are separate and can use or . Terminal rendering is broken Use a modern terminal with raw input and color support. Non-interactive environments should use or instead of the Ink UI. Links show URLs or will not open Terminal Markdown links intentionally display as rather than OSC8 hyperlinks, including in Cursor and macOS Terminal. Bare URLs are shown once, and detected URL fragments remain clickable when wrapped. Click the visible URL, not just its descriptive label. Agav tries first when configured, then the platform opener. On headless Linux without a display, the platform browser opener is unavailable; copy the URL into your local browser. If you still see garbled escape sequences in links, check that you are running an updated binary and report the terminal name and a minimal example. The startup logo looks wrong The startup banner is static, not a thinking animation or an image-protocol asset. It uses a 12×5 braille shell on macOS/Linux and a 16×7 block-character shell on Windows. If you see boxes or uneven cells, try a monospace terminal font that supports those characters. The name, version, and tagline stack below the mark on narrow terminals; the thinking spinner is unchanged. Gather diagnostics Run to inspect provider state, model, effort, sandbox backend, loaded tools, plugins, MCP connections, context use, and token accounting.

title: workflows
content: Workflows (experimental) Enable and in . is global-only and defaults off. A workflow is a JSON or YAML file describing a DAG of nodes. Every run executes in the background as a supervised runner job on the background-jobs coordinator, so it outlives the terminal or session that started it. Runs that need a human decision park and show up in an inbox that any session (CLI, slash command or TUI) can answer. Provider credentials are only needed when a run contains or nodes. title: Automation
content: Automation Repeat a prompt | Command | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Re-run a prompt in this session at the given interval. | | | Start a loop using the default 10 minute interval. | | | Stop the active in-session loop. | Use for an in-session interval: Use a positive whole number with (seconds), (minutes), (hours), or (days). Without a suffix, the interval is in minutes. The maximum is 2,147,483,647 ms (about 24.9 days); an interval above this limit is rejected without replacing the current loop. A valid new loop replaces the old one and first submits after one interval. with no arguments shows the prompt, interval, tick count, and elapsed time. stops future submissions; it does not cancel a turn already submitted. Loops stop when the interactive UI exits. Schedule persistent tasks | Command | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Open the schedule manager (list tasks in headless mode). | | | Save a recurring task using a five-field cron schedule. | | | Show saved scheduled tasks and their state. | | | Change an existing task's schedule, prompt, or both. | | | Pause the scheduled task identified by . | | | Resume the scheduled task identified by . | | | Delete the scheduled task identified by . | Scheduled tasks persist in ( on Windows). Use to find the ID of the task you want to update: An update requires at least one of or . Omit a flag to leave that value unchanged; an empty or whitespace-only prompt is rejected. Use the full ID or a unique prefix: an exact match takes precedence, and a prefix matching multiple tasks is rejected. Updating a task preserves its ID, display name, enabled or disabled state, creation time, and last-run time. Quote the cron expression. Put last to enter free-form text without quotes. If comes first, quote its text (unquoted text before is rejected): . Both and validate the complete cron expression before saving it: five fields in the order , with valid field values, ranges, and steps. Fields support wildcards (), lists (), ranges (), and steps (). Wildcard steps in the day-of-month and month fields start at , not : matches days 1, 3, 5, and so on, or months January, March, May, and so on. The interactive scheduler polls every 30 seconds and checks for matches at most once per minute, using the machine’s local time. All five fields must match, including both day-of-month and day-of-week if both are restricted. is available during a turn; updates and other changes wait until Agav is idle. never installs an operating-system daemon, so Agav must be active when one of these tasks matches. To run shell commands on a schedule that keeps firing while Agav is closed, use background jobs instead: they can be driven by or . Watch files | Command | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Run when matching files change. | | | Show the active watcher. | | | Stop the active watcher. | On macOS and Linux, run a trusted, non-interactive shell command once before automating it. Then watch a directory or use a glob. The watch expression is one whitespace-delimited argument, so paths with spaces are not supported. Only one watcher can be active. Changes are debounced by 300 ms. Stopping or replacing the watcher discards a pending callback, even if the replacement fails to start. It does not terminate commands already launched. Watcher events containing , , or in the reported filename are ignored. Commands run from Agav’s working directory with a 30-second timeout; non-empty output goes to stderr under . Watch mode ends when the UI exits. Watch commands launch directly through , not through the sandbox and confirmation flow. Native Windows does not support this runner; switching the Python executable name or launching Agav from PowerShell does not change it. Use for repeated agent checks or a Windows-native file watcher for change-triggered checks. Use only trusted commands; avoid commands that deploy, modify data, or require interactive input. For headless jobs, prefer or from your existing CI scheduler.

title: Files and Context
content: Files and Context Mention files in prompts | Command or syntax | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Attach a cwd-relative file or directory to the prompt. | | | Attach a cwd-relative path whose name contains spaces. | | | Enter a literal without triggering a file mention. | Use cwd-relative references in interactive prompts, queries, and non-interactive modes: Agav resolves within the current working directory only. Absolute paths are rejected, and paths cannot escape through or symlinks. Agav supports at most five unique resolved paths per prompt; mentioning the same file more than once still counts as one attachment. Type for a literal . Text files are included directly when they are small enough. If a mentioned text file exceeds 500 lines or 100KB, Agav replaces the full contents with a structure outline and warning instead of silently flooding model context. In the terminal UI, paths support Tab completion, including directory completion with a trailing . Directory mentions are supported through only, not through . Directory context is non-recursive: Agav inspects immediate files only, includes at most 20 files, and shows at most 100 lines per text file. Documents and images The tool and file mentions understand: - text files, with optional inclusive line ranges - images, returned as compressed visual previews - PDFs, with inclusive page ranges of up to ten pages - Word and PowerPoint documents (, , , ) For text files, accepts absolute or relative paths and inclusive, one-based and bounds. Omit for default UTF-8 detection, or specify , , , or . Large reads return a bounded excerpt and, when possible, the next line to read in the original file. See Tool output limits. LibreOffice improves Office handling when it is installed locally, and you can point Agav to it with . Legacy and files require LibreOffice. Without LibreOffice, and fall back to text extraction only; keeps slide-based ranges, but does not preserve page ranges or layout. Vision content is useful only when the selected model can process images. Explore a repository without attaching files These are agent tools, not slash commands. Ask Agav to use them when you want a narrower view than an attachment: - : set to map source paths without opening files for symbol extraction. Set to include hidden source paths. - : set for paths relative to the search root, or to change the result cap. can filter by ( or ) and show dot-prefixed entries with . - : use for literal text, for case-insensitive matching, and for a basename glob. Use and for nearby lines or to change the match cap. - : select an inclusive one-based cell range with / and filter by (, , or ). For source only, set . See Built-in Tools for limits and options. Paste content Large text pastes become numbered attachments so the prompt stays readable. Text of 50 or more characters is converted into a pasted attachment; shorter text and single-line HTTP(S) URLs stay inline. Pasted line endings are normalized so multiline text keeps its separate lines. Paste the same text again immediately, without editing the prompt, to expand the latest attachment into editable text. The “paste again to expand” hint appears only while that action is available. Expansion opens at the beginning of the pasted text; use ↑/↓ to navigate its visual rows. Long input scrolls with the caret and shows the visible row range, so you can inspect and edit the full paste. Editing the prompt clears repeat-paste eligibility; pasting again then creates a new attachment. Paste an image from the clipboard to attach it when the terminal and operating system integration supports clipboard image extraction. Clipboard images are saved under in the working directory and rely on platform clipboard helpers: on macOS, or ; on Linux, (Wayland) or (X11). On native Windows, save the image as a local file and attach it with instead. Use to list registered session attachments and to open or preview one. Backspace immediately after an attachment label removes it before submission. Run a shell command At the Agav prompt, runs a command directly from the working directory, shows the raw output, and submits the command and output to the agent for analysis. Use it only for commands you intend to run yourself: unlike the tool, it runs outside the tool sandbox and inherits your environment. Agav uses for direct commands on macOS and Linux and on native Windows, even when you launched it from PowerShell. The tool also uses the backend’s shell, not your interactive shell. For example, to display a local log: | Where you type | Command | | --- | --- | | Agav prompt on macOS/Linux | | | Agav prompt on native Windows | | | Windows PowerShell, outside Agav | | Ask a side question | Command | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Start a short, independent background question without blocking the active task. | | | Ask an independent question with a specific local file attached. | | | Change the active task instead of asking an independent side question. | Use for a small, independent question while the main agent is working: supports the same expansion as a normal prompt and receives the active conversation as read-only context. It still runs as one separate provider call rather than through the main agent loop: it cannot use tools, plugins, MCP servers, skills, or project instructions. Attach a file when the side question needs exact local context. Its answer is intentionally brief, usually one to three sentences. Use instead when the new information should change the active task. Use a normal follow-up when the question depends on the shared conversation or needs a detailed answer.

title: Workflows
content: Workflows Agav supports short questions and longer SDLC work from the same terminal interface. - Files and context: attach code, documents, images, and pasted content. - Sessions and memory: resume sessions, fork conversations with , compact context, export chats, and preserve project knowledge. - Planning and steering: structure multi-step work and redirect an active task. - Automation: loop prompts, schedule tasks, and watch files. - Non-interactive and CI: run one-shot prompts with controlled stdout and permissions. For sensitive repositories, begin interactive work in read-only mode and move to normal confirmations when you are ready to make changes: For headless or CI-style audits, prefer an explicit tool policy:

title: Non-interactive and CI
content: Non-interactive and CI Agav provides two one-shot modes. Quote prompts that contain spaces. In print mode, pass the prompt immediately after ; put flags such as and before the pair. Both modes also accept piped stdin. When stdin is present, Agav wraps it as: and prepends it to the prompt it sends to the model. Print mode | Command | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Run one agent turn and write only the final answer to stdout. | | | Stream response text while preserving stderr for tool progress and errors. | runs one agent turn, writes the final answer to stdout, writes tool progress and errors to stderr, and exits: Pipe a text log from the shell that launches Agav: POSIX shell Windows PowerShell Print mode accepts cwd-relative mentions, but it does not add dynamic repository context such as git state, project instructions, memories, or skills. caps agent iterations for the print prompt. The cap applies per prompt across model requests, including retries. Run mode | Command | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Run a one-shot, repository-aware agent task with streamed output. | | | Limit the number of model requests available to the task. | | | Supply an explicit JSON tool-permission policy. | includes dynamic repository context and streams output, making it suitable for agent-style CI work: Non-interactive runs default to auto-accept, subject to organization policy. Use or with to narrow what CI jobs can do. Control tools with JSON permissions or : In Windows PowerShell, set the JSON in the environment instead of passing it as a native command argument. Restore or remove the variable after the run if the shell will be reused: An explicit allows the listed tools and blocks other tools that are not already safe. If a policy contains deny rules without , Agav falls back to broad -style blocking rather than fine-grained per-tool deny behavior. and apply to only, not to . You can also use the normal selection flags in non-interactive mode, including , , , , and the Ollama connection flags. Structured output | Command | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Require the final answer to match a JSON Schema file in the current directory. | | | Require the final answer to match an inline JSON Schema. | Require final stdout to match JSON Schema: In Windows PowerShell, prefer the quoted file form to avoid embedded JSON quotes in native arguments. is print-mode only. Schema mode buffers output even when is present. Agav validates JSON, retries once with correction instructions if the iteration budget allows, then prints only the validated JSON value. Invalid schemas, provider errors, or output that remains invalid return exit code ; success returns . Keep secrets in environment variables and use an appropriately narrow tool policy for CI jobs. Trajectory export Use to save a one-shot transcript separately from stdout. Both examples work in a POSIX shell or Windows PowerShell: The versioned JSON records the provider, model, timestamps, aggregate token usage (including cache reads and writes), and ordered messages with tool calls and results. It keeps the recorded history through compaction and retries. It may contain prompts, file contents, and tool output: image bytes are omitted, but secrets are not redacted. Write to a protected location and review before sharing. The destination’s parent directory must already exist. Agav attempts to write completed history even on provider or output-schema validation failure; a startup failure or hard kill may leave no file. An export write failure is reported on stderr and returns exit code . The flag does not change stdout formatting and is not supported in interactive mode. Output recovery and stopping jobs Model-facing tool text has the same output limits as interactive sessions, even with . Streaming the final answer does not make intermediate tool results unlimited. Saved output paths are temporary and normal process exit attempts cleanup; ask Agav to copy required diagnostics into a protected artifact location during the run, before it exits. A saved log can itself be partial. Non-interactive tasks have no Ink selection/copy shortcuts or stay-in-session Esc behavior. Use your scheduler's timeout and termination policy, and do not assume a hard-killed process can finish cleanup or publish its logs. Native shell cleanup is best-effort; agent/test subprocesses, detached jobs, MCP server work, and Docker containers have different cancellation limits. Arrange explicit service/container cleanup in CI rather than relying on universal descendant termination. See cancellation limits.

title: Planning and Steering
content: Planning and Steering Plans | Command or prompt | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Require Agav to create a structured plan before it starts the request. | | | Show this session's plan, its step states, and recorded verification commands. | | | List every plan saved for the current project, across all sessions. | | | Manually set step to , , , or . | | | Remove this session's plan when it is no longer useful. | | or | Ask Agav to execute a request directly without creating a plan. | | | Toggle the plan detail panel to see descriptions and verify commands mid-run. | Prefix a request with to force a structured plan: Agav can also create a plan automatically for sufficiently complex refactors, migrations, or multi-phase work. Auto-generated plans usually contain 2 to 5 high-level steps. Plans are saved per-session under , anchored at the repository root. Agav works one step at a time, with step states , , , and . Plans belong to the session that created them and survive restarts. Resume a session with to pick its plan back up. Use to see all plans saved for the current project. Stale plans are automatically pruned after 30 days. and are explicit opt-ins. Agav also recognizes opt-outs such as , , , , and . Use to manually update a step, or press to view the full plan detail panel. Use the plan panel to check progress while a turn is running. and can also report progress mid-turn; edits such as or queue until idle. Use when you want to redirect the active work now. Non-interactive and do not create session plans or expose . Steering | Command | Intent | | --- | --- | | | Redirect the main agent, or only the inspected subagent, at its next safe step. | | | Show the active steering directives. | | | Remove the directive at . | | | Remove every active steering directive. | Steers redirect the active task within the same turn without rewriting the original request. Foreground main-agent directives can also be managed for subsequent turns: Use steering when constraints change mid-task or a deadline narrows the scope. It works during foreground turns and while attached to a live background worker, including after . Delivery happens at the next safe step, not by interrupting a tool already executing. From the overview, targets the main agent. Open a live subagent inspector to target only that child, then return with Tab to steer the main agent again. Main-agent directives are not inherited by children, and child directives do not go to the parent or siblings. Skill executions do not support steering. Foreground main-agent directives remain in memory for subsequent main-agent turns until removed; they are not restored as an active directive list in a later CLI process. Worker delivery instead uses a durable, execution-bound inbox for the selected recipient, not a saved list for future executions. In the foreground main view, bare behaves like . Bare , , , and are unavailable while attached to a worker or in a subagent inspector. Pause remains unsupported for worker-owned turns; see Detached sessions. Verify and revert edits For a targeted verification run, ask Agav to use with a test path and, if needed, up to (10 minutes). A timeout is a failed verification even if the partial output reports passing tests. Run to inspect the in-memory stack of tracked file changes, even during a turn. Once idle, run with the number from the current list to revert just that entry, or bare to revert the most recent tracked change. If the same text occurs several times in a file, ask the agent to target the specific one-based with rather than replacing every match. Independent subagents Agav may delegate self-contained work to parallel subagents. Each gets its own conversation context and the available tools, while confirmations remain visible in the main UI. Agav currently allows up to five concurrent subagents. Write-oriented subagents attempt to work in isolated Git worktrees and apply their changes back afterward; if the merge-back step fails, Agav reports a warning. See plugins and subagents for details.

title: Sessions and Memory

To keep a task executing after closing the UI, set in global config before submitting it and use or the configurable shortcut (default Ctrl+D); see Detached sessions. The resume picker also includes live runtimes and their pending approval counts. Workers checkpoint visible conversation history and token usage; live and saved session totals include subagent and skill usage. Resuming observes that progress without replaying the task. Ordinary or Ctrl+C requests durable, generation-bound cancellation of a selected worker; Esc requests cancellation without leaving Agav when no focused UI consumes it. Cancellation is asynchronous, not proof that all effects stopped. Switching sessions or unmounting the presentation does not cancel execution or answer approvals. There is no separate public session stop command; resume and interrupt instead. > Windows: paths resolve to . opens a picker listing all saved sessions, with the total count shown in the header. You can move the selection with , , or the mouse wheel, or click a row to resume it. Press to resume the selected session, to delete saved or terminal sessions (not active workers), or to rename active or terminal sessions, to start a new session instead of resuming one ( also works while typing in the search bar), and or to cancel. In the rename view, type the new name and press to save, or press to cancel and return to the list without renaming. Filter the picker by session name with or a click in its search bar. Outside search, cycles project scope, toggles updated/created sorting, and cycles all/running/needs-approval status filters. The running filter includes workers waiting for approval; an approval banner highlights sessions needing a decision. This name filter is separate from , which searches saved messages, names, and titles. Note: resuming a session created with keeps the session's own history but the turn cap is reapplied to each new prompt. A session also remembers its permission mode. It exports a snapshot of the committed, retained conversation at dispatch time, excluding in-flight streaming output and tool results not yet committed. It does not wait for the active turn to finish. Files are saved in the working directory as or . Sanitized filenames include . Existing files are never overwritten; collisions get a numeric suffix. The command reports the saved path or a useful failure message. New files request owner-only read/write permissions on POSIX; this does not configure Windows ACLs. Empty or internal-only conversations do not create files. Export never changes the active conversation or saved history. By default, Markdown retains the existing readable layout, with previews of tool inputs (200 characters) and results (500 characters). JSON preserves the full retained message structure, text, and tool activity without those additional preview limits. Both exclude agent-injected internal prompts while preserving actual user messages. skips messages copied into the active branch by . It works with Markdown, JSON, Markdown, and . Markdown includes the branch session ID in the header. JSON sets to and includes . Root sessions, older branches without recorded fork metadata, and branches with no new retained messages produce a message instead of a file. Review exports before sharing because new replies can still quote earlier context. Exports cover the retained conversation, not a complete session archive. For a one-shot CLI run instead, see Trajectory export. Context management may already have trimmed tool results or replaced old messages with a summary. Export cannot recover discarded content; a known compaction is reported in command feedback and JSON metadata. Expanded file attachments and per-turn environment context may be present in JSON, even when the terminal shows only a shorter display label. JSON format The UTF-8 file is indented JSON with a trailing newline: - and identify the current selection. , when available, contains tracked session totals, potentially spanning model switches and messages no longer retained. It is not usage per exported message. Missing usage is omitted, not estimated. - records known conversation compaction. does not guarantee that no tool results have been trimmed. - preserve order and roles, with blocks for text, tool calls, tool results, and images. Tool call/result IDs, names, structured inputs, error flags, and nested are retained. Optional , , and describe presentation and invocation. - Unsanitized JSON includes available base64 and media/dimension metadata; image-heavy exports can be large. Sanitized JSON replaces image bytes with , retains media/dimension metadata, and reports the omitted payload count. Images are not reopened, uploaded or analyzed. - Opaque provider replay metadata is excluded in either mode; counts blocks where it was removed. The file is for reading and processing, not a provider replay checkpoint or an import/resume guarantee. Sanitization limits Sanitization runs locally before writing, across message text, display/source text, nested tool inputs/results, and included textual metadata. The original conversation remains unchanged, and no raw intermediate export is written. The same rules apply to Markdown and JSON; Markdown redaction happens before preview truncation. Supported rules mask recognizable , GitHub //// and tokens (at least eight token characters after the prefix), bearer credentials, and string values assigned to recognizable credential names such as , , , , , , , , and . Common underscore-prefixed environment names such as are recognized too. The replacement is . Terminal presentation controls are removed before matching, and the current user's home path is shortened to at path boundaries, including Windows separator and case variants. Ordinary long strings and hashes are not automatically treated as secrets. Review before sharing. This is a best-effort aid, not a guarantee: arbitrary secrets, PII, encoded credentials, unsupported formats, secrets in object keys, and other users' paths can remain. Object keys and non-string values are preserved. Image contents cannot be inspected by text redaction, so image payloads are omitted from sanitized JSON. A successful sanitized export does not certify that it is safe to publish. Run to force compaction. Use to see what the context window currently holds. Its Used and Free rows are an estimate of current occupancy, not cumulative token usage. The session totals it also lists add up every request in the session, so they can exceed the context window. While a turn is running, is a snapshot of committed messages and excludes the output still being generated. When a compaction summary exists, press in the UI to show or hide it.
